items.title: Sound Reactor Mission: Gamified Misophonia Assessment to Bridge the Gap in Audiology and Hearing Care
items.authors: Jorge Mejia(National Acoustic Laboratories); Jan-Willem Wasmann(Radboud University Medical Center); Jane Gregory(University of Oxford)
items.abstract: Misophonia causes strong emotional and physiological reactions to specific everyday sounds, yet audiology lacks a standardised, scalable assessment pathway. Sound Reactor Mission (SRM) is a browser-based, gamified speech-in-noise assessment requiring only headphones. In a six-minute space mission, participants complete adaptive Speech Reception Threshold estimation, select a personally annoying masker, compare speech intelligibility across three masker conditions, and complete an Acceptable Noise Level measure. Pilot data (N = 14; 100% completion; mean time = 6.5 min) showed lower intelligibility for the selected annoying sound (59.2%) than for synthetic (71.7%) and standard masking noise (86.3%). The live Interspeech demonstration lets attendees complete the mission and compare their results with other delegates.

items.title: An Immersive VR System for Experiencing Spatial Speech-in-Noise Challenges in Clinical Audiology
items.authors: Nicky Chong-White(National Acoustic Laboratories); Thomas Ho(National Acoustic Laboratories)
items.abstract: Clinical hearing test results can be difficult for patients and families to connect with real-world listening difficulties, making it harder to explain why everyday communication is challenging and how hearing devices and strategies can help. This paper presents a VR-based immersive listening demonstration system on Apple Vision Pro that allows patients to experience common listening challenges directly. The system places users in one of three 3D environments (café, train station, and living room) with a target speaker, competing talkers, and spatially rendered environmental noise. Users listen to short dialogues and answer comprehension questions, while clinicians configure difficulty through presets that vary signal-to-noise ratio, source count, and spatial separation. The system is designed as a portable clinical demonstration tool, not a diagnostic assessment.

items.title: ELSI: An Interface for Standardizing Child-Centered Datasets, Applying Machine Learning Models, and Extracting Metrics
items.authors: Kaveri K. Sheth(Ecole Normale Supérieure); Loann Peurey(Ecole Normale Supérieure); Sho Tsuji(Ecole Normale Supérieure); Alejandrina Cristia(Ecole Normale Supérieure)
items.abstract: The ExELang Legacy Support Interface (ELSI) is an open-source interface designed to support researchers studying language acquisition in diverse communities around the world. ELSI enables users, regardless of technical expertise, to standardize child-centered datasets, apply machine learning models trained on child-centered audio (e.g., speaker diarization, phoneme counts), and extract key metrics such as child vocalization count, adult vocalization count, and conversational turns. During the Show and Tell, we will demonstrate how to use the interface by walking through dataset standardization, model execution, and metric extraction. We expect ELSI to be particularly valuable for researchers who maintain large child-centered audio datasets and wish to leverage open-source machine learning tools without requiring advanced programming skills.

items.title: Demonstration of Embedded Systems for Clinical Speech Analysis
items.authors: Jeremiah B Joyce(Mayo Clinic); Erik Clemens(Mayo Clinic); Sanjeev Mishra(Mayo Clinic); Josh Boesche(Mayo Clinic); David Johnson(Mayo Clinic); Marie Reyes(Mayo Clinic)
items.abstract: Interest in applying computational speech analysis tools for clinical purposes has grown alongside improvements in software. However, many existing tools rely on specialized hardware uncommon in routine clinical settings, separating data collection, analysis, and reporting in both time and space. Embedded systems can integrate sensors, graphics processing units, and displays into a single bedside platform, enabling speech analysis at the point of care. This approach could provide timely results that can be incorporated into urgent clinical decision-making. Here, we demonstrate the novel use of an embedded system to execute the core components of a computational speech analysis pipeline currently used to evaluate patients with psychiatric disorders, enabling end-to-end processing directly at the bed-side.

items.title: The TinyExplorer Ecosystem: Open tools for studying infants’ auditory and visual experiences
items.authors: Cátia M Oliveira(Cardiff University); Teodor Y. Nikolov(Cardiff University); Tamas Foldes(University of Surrey); Charlotte Bocchetta(Cardiff University); Hana D'Souza(Cardiff University)
items.abstract: Studying young children’s everyday learning environments remains difficult because existing methods often fail to capture the dynamic, multimodal, and socially embedded nature of children’s experiences in naturalistic settings. Recent advances in technology, including more user-friendly hardware and AI-powered software, are creating new opportunities to study young children’s everyday auditory and visual experiences in rich and scalable ways by utilising head-mounted cameras (headcams). However, the widespread use of headcams in research is still limited by two major barriers: (a) developing safe, lightweight, child-friendly recording systems, and (b) the time-intensive process of manual audio and video annotation. The TinyExplorer Ecosystem is an open-source platform designed to address these challenges by combining wearable egocentric recording hardware (TinyExplorer Gear) with locally run AI-powered annotation tools (TinyExplorer Detection App). The TinyExplorer Detection App currently integrates automated face detection and is being expanded to include hand detection, hand-object interaction annotation, and audio processing. Together, these tools support scalable, reproducible research on children’s real-world learning environments.

items.title: Head-Worn Dipole Microphone Array-based Speech Enhancement System for Single-Sided Deafness
items.authors: Ken Takaki(The University of Tokyo); Kouei Yamaoka(The University of Tokyo); Yoshihiro Kawahara(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: People with single-sided deafness (SSD) struggle to hear on their deaf side. However, conventional hearing aids typically have forward directionality to enhance speech from the front of the listener, making them poorly suited to SSD users, who need improved intelligibility of lateral speech. This gap motivates dedicated hardware and signal processing for hearing aids targeting the lateral direction. In this work, we construct a MEMS dipole microphone array with a side-directed beam to enhance sounds arriving laterally. We measured the array's transfer functions on a dummy head and simulated a noisy scenario. Beamforming with an array of two dipole and one omnidirectional microphones improved SDR by 0.78 dB and ESTOI by 0.04 for lateral speech, compared to a 3-channel omnidirectional array colocated. Our show-and-tell features audio demos and live real-time beamforming to show the potential of dipole microphones for this application and raise awareness of SSD in the community.

items.title: BetterSpeak: An Atypical Speech to Typical Speech Platform for Dysarthric Speakers
items.authors: Seyed Reza Shahamiri(University of Auckland); Zihan Zhong(University of Auckland); Qianli Wang(University of Auckland); Satwinder Singh(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems offer immense potential for individuals with dysarthria, yet traditional models fail severely due to high inter- and intra-speaker variability and data scarcity. To address this, we present BetterSpeak, a mobile ASR platform powered by our novel Two-Phase Personalized Conformer Adaptation Pipeline. The pipeline employs a resource-efficient transfer learning strategy, first adapting a robust Conformer model to the general dysarthric vocabulary, and then rapidly personalizing its acoustic encoder using limited, publicly available dysarthric speech samples. We detail the platform's functionalities and demonstrate how this personalized, data-efficient approach is crucial for providing children with an accessible, high-accuracy medium for communication, thereby fostering a better social and digital life.

items.title: ClinAware: Speech Enhancement Needs Clinical Awareness
items.authors: Pramod H. Kachare(Infosys Limited); Chetana Amancharla(Infosys Limited)
items.abstract: Speech enhancement is widely used to improve speech intelligibility in noisy conditions, while speech is increasingly investigated as a non-invasive modality for neurological applications. In telehealth and home-based assessments, speech enhancement is used as a preprocessing step. Its effects on clinically relevant speech biomarkers remain poorly understood. This demonstration presents an interactive system that allows users to explore the effect of speech enhancement methods on neurological voice biomarkers and a downstream risk indicator. Simulating a noisy environment or using noisy speech input, multiple enhancement methods are compared through spectrogram visualizations, quantitative biomarker changes, and corresponding shifts in a lightweight, interpretable risk score. The demo highlights that speech intelligibility improvement does not necessarily imply biomarker preservation, and it motivates a clinically informed design for future enhancements.

items.title: What does it mean to ‘know a word’?
AI in Communication Sciences: Necessity, Opportunity or Threat?
items.presenter: John H. L. Hansen, Emma Power, Visar Berisha, Karen Hirschausen, Brendan Lonergan, Nicky Chong-White (Facilitator)
items.abstract: Bringing together experts from research and clinical practice, this session will put the opportunities, risks and realities of AI in speech pathology and audiology up for debate. From its potential to improve care and accessibility to the ethical, professional and implementation challenges it presents, expect differing perspectives, challenging questions and a lively debate on what AI should, and should not, mean for the future of the field.

items.title: Relating the Neural Representations of Vocalized, Mimed, and Imagined Speech
items.authors: Maryam Maghsoudi(University of Maryland); Rupesh Chillale(University of Maryland); Shihab A Shamma(University of Maryland)
items.abstract: We investigated the relationship among neural representations of vocalized, mimed, and imagined speech recorded using publicly available stereotactic EEG recordings. Most prior studies have focused on decoding speech responses within each condition separately. Here, instead, we explore how responses across conditions relate by training linear spectrogram reconstruction models for each condition and evaluate their generalization across conditions. We demonstrate that linear decoders trained on one condition generally transfer successfully to others, implying shared speech representations. This commonality was assessed with stimulus-level discriminability by performing a rank-based analysis demonstrating preservation of stimulus-specific structure in both within- and across-conditions. Finally, we compared linear reconstructions to those from a nonlinear neural network. While both exhibited cross-condition transfer, linear models achieve superior stimulus-level discriminability.

items.title: Subject-Invariant Dynamic Graph Modeling for Cross-Subject EEG Imagined Speech Decoding
items.authors: Saravanakumar Duraisamy(University of Luxembourg); Luis A. Leiva(University of Luxembourg)
items.abstract: Decoding imagined speech using EEG-based Brain-Computer Interfaces suffers from substantial performance degradation when applied to unseen subjects due to strong inter-subject variability. We propose a subject-invariant dynamic graph modeling framework for cross-subject EEG-based imagined speech decoding. The method integrates multi-view dynamic connectivity priors with channel-wise graph attention and incorporates adversarial subject disentanglement using a gradient reversal layer to suppress subject-specific information. Evaluation under a strict leave-one-subject-out protocol across 15 subjects achieves average classification accuracies of 31.20% ± 3.12% and 30.36% ± 4.05% on two independent datasets. The results demonstrate consistent cross-subject generalization and highlight the importance of structured connectivity modeling and subject-invariant training for robust EEG-based speech decoding.

items.title: Exploiting EEG-based Gamma-Band Time Frequency Feature in WaveNet Decoder Framework for High-Fidelity Speech Reconstruction
items.authors: Rantu Buragohain(Indian Institute of Technology Jammu); Saket Maheshwari(GLA University); Karan Nathwani(Indian Institute of Technology Jammu)
items.abstract: This paper presents a novel speech synthesis framework that reconstructs audible speech directly from invasive electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, enabling a communication option for individuals with severe speech difficulties. The framework exploits time-frequency features extracted from the high-gamma band (70-170 Hz), strongly linked to speech production and perception, and maps them to speech representations using a WaveNet-based decoder. This framework comprises stacked causal dilated convolutional residual blocks with gated activations to capture both short-term articulatory patterns and long-range temporal relationships while maintaining causality. Residual and skip connections enhance feature propagation and stabilize training. Experimental results demonstrate strong correlations between predicted and actual spectrograms, highlighting both robustness and inter-subject variability, thereby advancing state-of-the-art neural speech decoding for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

items.title: More than a feeling: Expressive style influences cortical speech tracking in subjective cognitive decline
items.authors: Matthew King-Hang Ma(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yun Feng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Cloris Pui-Hang Li(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Manson Cheuk-Man Fong(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
items.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) doubles dementia risk. This study investigates how self-perceived cognitive worsening shapes neural dynamics during naturalistic speech perception. EEG was collected from 60 cognitively normal older adults as they listened to speech varied in prosodic contexts, categorized by expressive style (scrambled, descriptive, dialogue, exciting). Encoding models mapping three speech representations—acoustic, subsyllabic segmentation and phonotactic features—to ongoing EEG signals were built. Cortical tracking strength (CTS) showed that models fitted with subsyllabic linguistic features outperformed acoustic ones. Crucially, greater SCD severity was associated with weaker CTS of (1) subsyllabic linguistic but not acoustic features, and (2) prosodically flat speech (scrambled and descriptive). Thus, the CTS of higher-level linguistic features while listening to prosodically flat speech may serve as a potential neural marker for early-stage cognitive decline.

items.title: Bayesian Generalized Additive Multilevel Models for Accurate ERP Latency Estimation under Moderate Downsampling
items.authors: Zixia Fan(Macquarie University); Ronny Kurniawan Ibrahim(Macquarie University); Joshua Penney(Macquarie University); Felicity Cox(Macquarie University)
items.abstract: Estimating when event-related potential (ERP) effects begin and end helps characterize the timing of neural processing, but fitting single-trial Bayesian Generalized Additive Multilevel Models (GAMMs) at high sampling rates is computationally demanding. Downsampling can reduce this burden, but balancing accurate latency estimation with manageable computational cost is a key challenge. This study compared ERP latency estimates derived from Bayesian GAMMs across sampling rates, from full resolution down to an extreme downsampled rate, in a passive oddball paradigm. The mismatch negativity latency remained stable from full to moderate resolutions, with little shift in onset. In contrast, the late discriminative negativity showed a later onset and shorter duration as the sampling rate decreased. At the extreme resolution, both components remained detectable, but with reduced temporal precision. Overall, downsampling can reduce computational cost, but extreme downsampling should be avoided.

items.title: DisenEEG-Net: Disentangling EEG features via sufficient information bottleneck and adversarial learning for cross-subject auditory attention detection
items.authors: Tasleem Kausar(CUHK-Shenzhen); Yuan Liao(CUHK-Shenzhen); Haoqi Hu(CUHK-Shenzhen); Siqi Cai(HIT Shenzhen); Haizhou Li(CUHK-Shenzhen)
items.abstract: Cross-subject generalization remains a major challenge in EEG-based Auditory Attention Decoding (AAD), limiting the development of neuro-steered hearing devices. This challenge arises from large inter-subject variability in EEG signals and the difficulty of learning discriminative, subject-invariant representations. We propose DisenEEG-Net, an end-to-end feature disentanglement framework based on information theory and adversarial learning. It employs a parallel Transformer encoder to extract latent EEG representations, which are then decomposed into orthogonal task- and subject-specific subspaces. A sufficient information bottleneck retains essential subject information while suppressing task leakage, and adversarial training enforces subject invariance in task features. A decoder preserves feature fidelity during disentanglement. Results show that our proposed DisenEEG-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance under cross-subject settings on the KUL, DTU, and AVED datasets.

items.title: ASR-Synchronized Speaker-Role Diarization
items.authors: Arindam Ghosh(Solventum Health Information Systems); Mark Fuhs(Solventum Health Information Systems); Bongjun Kim(Solventum Health Information Systems); Anurag Chowdhury(Solventum Health Information Systems); Monika Woszczyna(Solventum Health Information Systems, USA)
items.abstract: Speaker-role diarization (RD), e.g., doctor vs. patient, is often more practically useful than conventional speaker diarization (SD), which assigns generic labels, e.g., speaker-1, speaker-2. For joint ASR+RD, the current best model uses a single transducer to serially predict words and roles (at speaker turns), but at the cost of degraded ASR performance. To address this, we adapt a recent dual-transducer ASR+SD model for ASR+RD. We first show that SD and RD are fundamentally different tasks, exhibiting different dependencies on acoustic and linguistic cues. We then propose (1) task-specific predictors, (2) use of higher-layer ASR encoder features as input to the RD encoder, and (3) cross-entropy loss along the 1-best ASR path instead of the full RNNT loss. Experiments on a public and a private dataset of doctor-patient conversations show that our method outperforms the best baseline by relative 6.2% and 4.5%, respectively, in role-based word diarization error rate (R-WDER).

items.title: Delayed-Commitment Online Speaker Tracking for Robust Many-Speaker Diarization
items.authors: Youngki Kwon(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Hee-Soo Heo(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Minjae Lee(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Han-Gyu Kim(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Bong-Jin Lee(NAVER Cloud Corporation)
items.abstract: Online speaker diarization--determining "who spoke when" in real time--is critical for meeting transcription, yet scaling to many speakers remains challenging. Within the clustering paradigm, we propose an online diarization system with no explicit speaker-count cap. Its core module, Delayed-Commitment Online Speaker Tracking (DC-OST), labels each embedding immediately but defers new-speaker registration until sufficient evidence accumulates. DC-OST also incorporates an adaptive distance threshold to suppress spurious registrations. Under system voice activity detection, the proposed system achieves 9.53% and 9.12% DER at 0.5 s latency on VoxConverse and VoxSRC-23--up to 21 and 28 speakers, respectively--outperforming both DIART and Sortformer. Moreover, a per-speaker-count analysis shows that our system maintains consistent accuracy as the number of speakers grows, unlike baseline systems whose performance degrades.

items.title: Multi-Speaker Embeddings With Weakly Supervised Speaker Activity Detection For Granular Speaker Diarization
items.authors: Jenthe Thienpondt(Ghent University); Kris Demuynck(Ghent University)
items.abstract: In this paper, we present a novel weakly supervised multi-speaker embedding model for extracting embeddings and corresponding frame-level voice and speaker activity from multi-speaker utterances. The proposed model has two major advantages compared to traditional cascaded and hybrid end-to-end diarization approaches. First, it removes the dependency and computational overhead of external VAD and speaker segmentation models in the diarization pipeline. Second, instead of relying on coarse speaker boundaries derived from overlapping window embeddings, our approach provides frame-level speaker boundaries for multiple speakers within each window, without relying on labeled frame-level training data. Our proposed system achieves an average relative improvement of 13.7% in confusion error rate over our previous speaker diarization system across the AMI, VoxConverse and DIHARD III benchmarks.

items.title: Neural Multichannel Distant Speaker Diarization and Source Separation with Beta Speaker Activity Prior
items.authors: Sicheng Mao(Telecom Paris); Mathieu Fontaine(Telecom Paris); Anthony Larcher(Universite du Mans); Roland Badeau(Telecom Paris)
items.abstract: Distant speaker diarization remains challenging due to adverse acoustic conditions, varying numbers of speakers and overlapping speech. While data-driven approaches have shown strong performance, model-driven methods offer a compelling alternative by leveraging spatial information from multichannel recordings. This paper is motivated to propose a Bayesian diarization model for a model-driven method called neural FCASA to enhance its robustness. Specifically, we propose a beta prior over speaker activity and hence a variational lower bound objective that can be seen as a regularized continuous speaker activity score in place of the original cross-entropy loss to train the diarization model. Our experiments show significant improvements in terms of Diarization Error Rate by at least 3% (16% relatively) and Jaccard Error Rate by at least 4% (20% relatively) on the AMI dataset compared to the baseline.

items.title: Two-Level Uncertainty Suppression for Robust Meeting Diarization
items.authors: Shuhei Asaka(Institute of Science Tokyo); Muhammad Shakeel(Honda Research Institute Japan); Chikara Maeda(Honda Research Institute Japan); Benjamin Yen(Institute of Science Tokyo); Takeshi Ashizawa(Institute of Science Tokyo); Naoaki Sumida(Honda Research Institute Japan); Kazuhiro Nakadai(Institute of Science Tokyo)
items.abstract: Real-meeting diarization is challenged by uncertainty propagation, where boundary ambiguity from rapid speaker turns and overlap destabilizes downstream speaker assignment. We propose a two-level uncertainty suppression framework. For segmentation, linguistically contextualized representations from an OWSM-Encoder are integrated into WavLM via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) reducing boundary ambiguity in high-activity regions. For clustering, Known-Seed Guided Clustering (KSGC) leverages known-speaker embeddings to stabilize global assignment under mixed known/unknown-speaker conditions. On AMI, AliMeeting, and AISHELL-4, FiLM reduces DER by up to 1.8 points over WavLM-large, with largest gains in boundary-ambiguous scenarios. KSGC further improves DER by up to 2.62 points under mixed conditions, especially in meetings with frequent speaker turns. These results suggest that addressing uncertainty-related errors at complementary levels improves robustness in meeting diarization.

items.title: Hierarchical Permutation Consistency Learning for Self-Conditioned End-to-End Speaker Diarization
items.authors: Bongsu Jung(Incheon National University); Wooil Kim(Incheon National University)
items.abstract: Self-conditioned (SC) end-to-end neural diarization (EEND) iteratively refines speaker predictions across layers. However, conventional layer-wise permutation invariant training (PIT) independently determines the optimal speaker permutation at each layer. This layer-specific permutation selection causes hierarchical permutation inconsistency (HPI), propagating permutation noise into the SC path and disrupting training stability. To resolve this, we propose two frameworks: Group-Wise PIT (GW-PIT) and Continuous Influence PIT (CI-PIT). While GW-PIT enforces a global permutation constraint, CI-PIT applies soft regularization by aggregating layer-wise cost matrices using Gaussian weighting. This promotes permutation consistency across the hierarchy while preserving local representation flexibility. Experimental results on CALLHOME demonstrate that the proposed CI-PIT suppresses permutation noise, stabilizes training dynamics, and achieves DER improvements for 2- and 3-speaker scenarios.

items.title: SAM: A Mamba-2 State-Space Audio-Language Model
items.authors: Taehan Lee(Sogang University); Jaehan Jung(Sogang University); Hyukjun Lee(Sogang University)
items.abstract: We present SAM, a State-space Audio-language Model that integrates an audio encoder with a Mamba-2 backbone. SAM-2.7B achieves 21.1 mAP on AudioSet and 17.6 SPICE on AudioCaps, matching or surpassing larger 7B transformer-based models with fewer parameters. We further provide the first systematic, representation-level analysis of how SSMs interact with audio encoder outputs: (1) joint audio encoder finetuning is essential, supported by accuracy gains and observed adaptation of token representation rank and similarity across different SSM sizes; (2) despite linear scaling, SSMs benefit more from compact, information-rich audio token representations than from excessively long token sequences; and (3) incorporating instruction-following supervision substantially improves reasoning ability, boosting MMAU-Sound accuracy from 22.8 to 56.8. Through comprehensive experiments and analysis, we establish practical design principles for SSMs as strong, scalable backbones for audio-language models.

items.title: Samsone: A Family of Open Small Audio Language Models for On-Device Inference
items.authors: Piotr Masztalski(Samsung R&D Institute Poland; AGH University of Kraków); Michal K. Grzeszczyk(Samsung R&D Institute Poland); Olaf Sikorski(Samsung R&D Institute Poland)
items.abstract: The success of Large Audio Language Models has driven the development of massive multimodal networks exceeding billions of parameters. However, the demand for privacy-preserving, low-latency processing has shifted focus toward Small Audio Language Models (SALMs) capable of on-device execution. In this paper, we introduce Samsone, a family of SALMs designed for edge computing. Our core model, Samsone-134M, establishes a new state-of-the-art for its size class across multiple benchmarks. We further explore the scaling laws of SALMs by introducing Samsone-99M and Samsone-356M. Despite their compact footprint, the Samsone family delivers performance competitive with models orders of magnitude larger. To foster open research and reproducibility, we train Samsone on publicly available data. We release the training code, model weights, mobile-optimized checkpoints and provide an open-source Android application to demonstrate real-time on-device inference of Samsone.

items.title: FreeSonic: Training-Free Temporal-Aware Decoupled Attention for Precise Audio Editing
items.authors: Yuxuan Jiang(Tsinghua University); Mingyang Han(Alibaba Group); Yusheng Dai(Monash University); Andong Wang(Renmin University of China); Tianhong Zhou(Tsinghua University); Jiaxin Ye(Fudan University); Dongxiao Wang(Alibaba Group); Haoxiang Shi(Alibaba Group); Boyu Li(Alibaba Group); Jun Song(Alibaba Group); Cheng Yu(Alibaba Group); Bo Zheng(Alibaba Group); Weibei Dou(Tsinghua University); Zehua Chen(Tsinghua University); Jun Zhu(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Text-to-audio (TTA) generation has made significant strides, yet achieving precise and consistent audio editing remains a major challenge. However, existing methods struggle to balance temporal consistency with background preservation. In this paper, we propose FreeSonic, a training-free framework leveraging the state-of-the-art Rectified Flow-based TangoFlux model. FreeSonic utilizes an optimized inversion-reverse process and joint text-audio attention maps for precise target segment extraction. For content editing, a novel scheduled attention decoupling confines modifications to target regions while preserving original acoustic context. Furthermore, task-oriented noise injection enhances versatility for tasks such as audio removal and non-rigid replacement. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that FreeSonic achieves a superior balance by providing a high-fidelity and efficient solution for precise and consistent audio editing. Project and demos: https://free-sonic.github.io/.

items.title: Resonate: Reinforcing Text-to-Audio Generation via Online Feedback from Large Audio Language Models
items.authors: Xiquan Li(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Junxi Liu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Wenxi Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Haina Zhu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Ziyang Ma(X-LANCE Lab, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Xie Chen(X-LANCE Lab, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute)
items.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an effective paradigm for enhancing Large Language Models (LLMs) and visual generative models. However, its application in text-to-audio (TTA) generation remains largely under-explored. Prior work typically employs offline methods like Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and leverages Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP) models as reward functions. In this study, we investigate the integration of online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) into TTA generation. We adapt the algorithm for Flow Matching-based audio models and demonstrate that online RL significantly outperforms its offline counterparts. Furthermore, we incorporate rewards derived from Large Audio Language Models (LALMs), which can provide fine-grained scoring signals that are better aligned with human perception. With only 470M parameters, our final model, Resonate, establishes a new SOTA on TTA-Bench in terms of both audio quality and semantic alignment.

items.title: GACA-DiT: Diffusion-based Dance-to-Music Generation with Genre-Adaptive Rhythm and Context-Aware Alignment
items.authors: Jinting Wang(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)); Yan Rong(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)); Chenxing Li(Tencent AI Lab); Li Liu(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
items.abstract: Dance-to-music (D2M) generation aims to compose music that is rhythmically and temporally aligned with dance. Prior methods rely on coarse rhythm embeddings (e.g., global motion features or binarized joint rhythms), which discard fine-grained motion cues and weaken alignment. In addition, temporal mismatches introduced by feature downsampling further impair synchronization. We propose GACA-DiT, a diffusion transformer-based framework for rhythm-consistent and temporally aligned music generation. It contains two key modules: (1) a Genre-Adaptive rhythm extraction module that integrates multi-scale temporal–spatial analysis with adaptive joint weighting to capture fine-grained, genre-aware rhythm patterns; and (2) a Context-Aware temporal alignment module that leverages learnable queries to align music latents with relevant dance rhythms. Experiments on AIST++ and TikTok demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both objective metrics and human evaluation.

items.title: Rethinking Speech Foundation Model Fine-tuning: Better SFT or Better Match?
items.authors: Wangjin Zhou(Kyoto University); Yizhou Zhang(Kyoto University); Yichi Wang(Kyoto University); Tatsuya Kawahara(Kyoto University)
items.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely used to adapt self-supervised speech representations to downstream classification tasks. Small gains observed under a single pretrained checkpoint are often interpreted as method-level improvements, i.e., a higher attainable performance ceiling. We show that such conclusions are not always reliable because SFT outcomes depend strongly on the specific pretrained instance. We conduct a systematic study on three SUPERB classification tasks, evaluating eight SFT variants across nine pretrained checkpoints from wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, and WavLM, with multi-seed repetitions on representative base-scale models. We find that the identity of the statistically indistinguishable top-group SFT recipe is often checkpoint-dependent, with limited transferability across pretrained instances. These findings suggest that many reported downstream gains reflect instance and seed dependent elicitation match, rather than universally improving the attainable performance ceiling.

items.title: FlowEdit: Associative Memory for Lifelong Pronunciation Adaptation in Flow-Matching TTS
items.authors: Harshit Singh(University Of Maryland); Ayush Pratap Singh(TU Darmstadt); Nityanand Mathur(Smallest AI)
items.abstract: Flow-matching text-to-speech systems achieve remarkable zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment: pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist unless the model is retrained. We introduce FlowEdit, a lifelong adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits rather than weight updates. When corrective feedback is provided, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space, then stores the correction in a Modern Hopfield Network serving as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching. On our curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Corrections complete in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.

items.title: Privacy and quality trade-off in real-time speaker anonymization via editing of age and sex attributes
items.authors: Waris Quamer(Texas A&M University); Ricardo Gutierrez-Osuna(Texas A&M University)
items.abstract: Speaker anonymization aims to alter attributes in the speech signal to hide the identity of the speaker. While such attribute modifications can effectively hide speaker identity, they often degrade the quality of the synthesized speech. In this work, we present a systematic analysis of the privacy-quality trade-off by isolating two key attributes (age and sex) in a streaming speech synthesis system. We use objective metrics (speaker cosine similarity as a proxy of identity and DNS-MOS for speech quality) and perform linear regression to quantify how attribute shifts impact privacy and quality, and validate these trends with perceptual listening tests. Our results reveal that privacy degrades faster than quality as modifications increase, giving rise to an optimal anonymization region where moderate attribute changes achieve effective identity suppression with minimal naturalness loss. These findings provide actionable guidance for tuning any attribute-based anonymization system.

items.title: RIVET: Robust Idempotent Voice Attribute Editing
items.authors: Dareen Alharthi(Carnegie Mellon University); Bhuvan Koduru(Carnegie Mellon University); Rita Singh(Carnegie Mellon University); Bhiksha Ramakrishnan(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: Voice attribute editing models modify characteristics such as age and gender while preserving speaker identity. In large-scale speech datasets, however, attribute annotations are often noisy or inconsistent, which can cause conditional generative models to produce unstable edits. In this work, we show that idempotency provides an effective mechanism for improving robustness to noisy labels. An idempotent operator is one for which repeated application does not change the result, i.e., f(f(x)) = f(x). Enforcing this property acts as an implicit regularizer that reduces sensitivity to mislabeled examples. We introduce RIVET, a training framework that incorporates an idempotency objective to improve robustness to label noise. We evaluate RIVET under controlled label noise and on the GLOBE dataset with naturally noisy annotations. RIVET im-proves editing success and better preserves speaker identity than standard training, showing that idempotency improves robustness in voice editing models. Code is available online.

items.title: FineCombo-TTS: Collaborative and Precise Controllable Speech Synthesis Using Text Descriptions and Reference Speech
items.authors: Shuoyi Zhou(Tsinghua University); Yixuan Zhou(Tsinghua University); Peiji Yang(Tencent); Yifan Hu(Inner Mongolia University); Yicheng Zhong(Tencent); Zhisheng Wang(Tencent); Zhiyong Wu(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Controllable text-to-speech (TTS) has become a key research focus. However, methods based on either reference speech or text descriptions lack flexibility and precise control, and recent joint approaches remain loosely coupled, with speech modeling timbre and text controlling global style. We propose FineCombo-TTS, a unified framework for speech synthesis grounded in reference speech and guided by text descriptions, enabling flexible and precise control over acoustic attributes. Instead of explicit attribute disentanglement, we learn a unified acoustic representation and introduce a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM)-based Speech Variance Predictor to model fine-grained reference-to-target transformations guided by text descriptions. To support relative attribute control, we construct FineEdit, a structured paired dataset that explicitly encodes source-to-target attribute variations. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves flexible, precise, and expressive controllable TTS.

items.title: Edit Content, Preserve Acoustics: Imperceptible Text-Based Speech Editing via Self-Consistency Rewards
items.authors: Yong Ren(Chinese Academy of Sciences; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Jiangyan Yi(Tsinghua University); Jianhua Tao(Tsinghua University); Tao Wang(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Le Xu(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Zhengqi Wen(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Imperceptible text-based speech editing modifies spoken content through transcript manipulation while preserving acoustic continuity. Prior acoustic-space approaches suffer from content–style entanglement, causing unstable generation and boundary artifacts. We introduce a framework guided by the principle 'Edit Content, Preserve Acoustics'. Editing is conducted in a stable semantic space, while acoustic realization is handled by a Flow Matching decoder. To ensure perceptual consistency, we propose Self-Consistency Rewards Group Relative Policy Optimization, which leverages a pre-trained Text-to-Speech model as an implicit critic, together with intelligibility and duration constraints. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art autoregressive and non-autoregressive baselines in intelligibility, robustness, and perceptual quality.

items.title: Bagpiper-Edit: Zero-Shot Open-Ended Audio Editing via Rich-Caption
items.authors: Xun Gong(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Jinchuan Tian(Carnegie Mellon University); Haoran Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); William Chen(Carnegie Mellon University); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University); Yamin Qian(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
items.abstract: Current text-guided audio editing methods rely on paired training data, predefined operation templates, and separate processing pipelines across speech, music, and sound. We present Bagpiper-Edit to enable open-ended audio editing via free-form natural language instructions. We reformulate audio editing as a rich-caption rewriting task by treating a rich caption as the semantic representation of an audio clip. The user request is translated into an edited caption, which then guides Bagpiper-Edit to generate the target edited audio with the original audio as contextual acoustic anchor. This unlocks the potential of free-form editing, and circumvents the need for paired audio-editing training data, enabling powerful zero-shot editing capabilities. Evaluations across speech, audio, and free-form editing show Bagpiper-Edit maintains good consistency to the original audio and achieves similar performance to other expert models in most cases. Demo: https://bagpiper-edit.github.io

title: Domain Adaptation & Accented ASR
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 8 - Oral 3 - Domain Adaptation & Accented ASR

items.title: SEA-MDD: Self-adapting Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis Models via Test-Time Training
items.authors: Minglin Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Helen Meng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: Mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) assists second language (L2) learners in improving pronunciation. However, the substantial variability in learner proficiency and the diverse mispronunciation types hinder the development of reliable MDD systems. Large-scale annotation to cover all mispronunciations is prohibitively expensive. To address this data scarcity, we propose SEA-MDD, a SElf-Adapting MDD method that leverages Test-Time Training (TTT) to effectively adapt trained models to new speech samples. Specifically, we integrate multilayer perceptron (MLP)-based TTT modules into Transformer blocks of wav2vec 2.0. The parameters of TTT modules are updated during both training and test time via self-supervised learning. This design enables trained models to adjust dynamically to novel inputs, mitigating performance degradation commonly observed in prior MDD models when exposed to diverse speech distributions. Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

items.title: Mixture-of-Accent-Adapters for Robust ASR: Injecting Accent Cues into Pretrained Whisper
items.authors: Mehedi Hasan Bijoy(Aalto University); Yaroslav Getman(Aalto University); Tamás Grósz(South East Technological University); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University)
items.abstract: Accented speech remains a key challenge for inclusive ASR, yet adapting large pretrained models often relies on costly full fine-tuning. Moreover, previous methods lack integration of accent-specific adapters, controlled encoder-level accent-cue injection, and multitask supervision for specialization regulation and gender information leakage mitigation. We propose Mixture-of-Accent-Adapters (MoAA), a novel adaptation framework for Whisper that enables on-demand specialization while defaulting to the frozen backbone when unnecessary. A pooled-state control bottleneck estimates accentedness, guiding accent-cue injection via weighted retrieval from a learnable soft accent codebook and routing lightweight accent-specialist adapters, while calibrating a gated blend with the backbone. An adversarial gender head reduces leakage, and reference-free hallucination suppression mitigates rare decoding artifacts. On AESRC benchmark, MoAA achieves 7.49% WER and 3.81% CER.

items.title: Contrastive Regularization for Accent-Robust ASR
items.authors: Van-Phat Thai(Air Traffic Management Research Institute, Nanyang Technological University); Aradhya Dhruv(Air Traffic Management Research Institute, Nanyang Technological University); Duc-Thinh Pham(Air Traffic Management Research Institute, Nanyang Technological University; Center of AI Research, VinUniversity); Sameer Alam(Air Traffic Management Research Institute, Nanyang Technological University)
items.abstract: ASR systems based on self-supervised acoustic pretraining and CTC fine-tuning achieve strong performance on native speech but remain sensitive to accent variability. We investigate supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) as a lightweight, accent-invariant auxiliary objective for CTC fine-tuning. An utterance-level contrastive loss regularizes encoder representations without architectural modification or explicit accent supervision. Experiments on the L2-ARCTIC benchmark show consistent WER reductions across multiple pretrained encoders, with up to 25—29% relative reduction under unseen-accent evaluation. Analysis using within-transcript cosine dispersion indicates that SupCon promotes more compact and stable representation geometry under accent variability. Overall, SupCon provides an effective and model-agnostic regularization strategy for improving accent robustness.

items.title: Exploring the potential and limitations of Model Merging for Multi-Domain Adaptation in ASR
items.authors: Carlos Carvalho(INESC-ID; Universidade de Lisboa); Francisco Teixeira(INESC-ID); Thomas Rolland(INESC-ID); Alberto Abad(INESC-ID; Universidade de Lisboa)
items.abstract: Model merging is a scalable alternative to multi-task training that combines the capabilities of multiple specialised models into a single model. This is particularly attractive for large speech foundation models, which are typically adapted through domain-specific fine-tuning, resulting in multiple customised checkpoints, for which repeating full fine-tuning when new data becomes available is computationally prohibitive. In this work, we study model merging for multi-domain ASR and benchmark 11 merging algorithms for 10 European Portuguese domains, evaluating in-domain accuracy, robustness under distribution shift, as well as English and multilingual performance. We further propose BoostedTSV-M, a new merging algorithm based on TSV-M that mitigates rank collapse via singular-value boosting and improves numerical stability. Overall, our approach outperforms full fine-tuning on European Portuguese while preserving out-of-distribution generalisation in a single model.

items.title: Activation Steering for Accent Adaptation in Large Audio Language Models
items.authors: Jinuo Sun(The University of Melbourne); Yang Xiao(The University of Melbourne); Sung Kyun Chung(The University of Melbourne); Qiuchi Hu(The University of Melbourne); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Eun-Jung Holden(The University of Melbourne); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: Accent variability remains a major source of errors in automatic speech recognition, yet most adaptation methods rely on parameter fine-tuning without understanding where accent information is encoded. We treat accent variation as an interpretable subspace in hidden representations and investigate whether it can be identified and controlled directly in activation space. We extract layer-wise encoder activations and estimate mean-shift directions capturing accent-induced representation shifts. By injecting these directions into individual layers and measuring how they align accented and standard embeddings, we derive a layer-wise accent sensitivity profile, revealing that accent information concentrates in a narrow band of middle encoder layers. Leveraging this structure, we further introduce parameter-free accent steering that modifies representations during inference without updating model weights. Experiments across eight accents show consistent word error rate reductions.

items.title: AccentDrift: Real-time Streaming Accent Conversion via Sparse Speech Tokenization
items.authors: Sang-Hoon Lee(Ajou University); Heejin Choi(Samsung Research); Joun Yeop Lee(Samsung Research); Sangjun Park(Samsung Research)
items.abstract: Although recent speech AI advances have enabled real-time speech understanding and generation, real-time accent conversion (AC) for second-language (L2) speakers in real-world interactions remains underexplored. In this paper, we present AccentDrift, a real-time streaming AC system that preserves linguistic content and speaker identity while transforming speech into a target accent with low latency. From an information bottleneck perspective, we adopt sparse speech tokenization to extract linguistic information from continuous speech. An accent adapter injects accent style into sparse semantic tokens, followed by a timbre adapter that hierarchically generates speaker-specific acoustics. To support streaming, we adopt a cache-aware streaming architecture and parallel streams, achieving 520 ms latency. AccentDrift outperforms prior parallel AC models, and demonstrates the feasibility of generating native-like accents for L2 speakers. Audio samples are available at https://accentdrift.github.io/demo/.

title: Multi-Speaker Processing, Personalization, and Adaptation
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 9 - Oral 5 - Multi-Speaker Processing, Personalization, and Adaptation

items.title: Mitigating Speaker Leakage in Cascaded Multi-talker ASR with Diarization-based Transcript Correction
items.authors: Hermann Yepdjio Nkouanga(Portland State University); Minwei Luo(Portland State University); Maggie Wigness(US Army Research Laboratory); Suresh Singh(Portland State University)
items.abstract: While cascaded multi-talker ASR (MT-ASR) leverages state-of-the-art foundation models, its performance is often capped by speaker leakage during separation. Prior correction strategies primarily focus on lexical re-labeling for speaker attribution. We propose a complementary pruning-based paradigm that robustly identifies and removes leakage artifacts. Our method utilizes a pre-trained speaker diarization model as a multimodal verifier to prune transcribed segments satisfying a tripartite consensus of temporal containment, lexical cross-validation, and temporal alignment. Results on LibriMix, LibriSpeechMix, and the AMI Meeting corpus show our algorithm consistently reduces cpWER across diverse overlap conditions. Specifically, on subsets with high speaker leakage, our method achieves relative cpWER reductions of up to 29%, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing the reliability of cascaded MT-ASR transcripts in complex acoustic environments.

items.title: Beyond Mimicry: Constrained Exploration with GRPO for Joint Multi-Talker ASR and Diarization under Unknown Speaker Counts
items.authors: Yunrui Cai(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Dingdong Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Lingwei Meng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xixin Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Zhiyong Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Tsinghua University); Helen Meng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: Joint multi-talker ASR with speaker attribution and timestamps is particularly challenging when the speaker count is unknown and the output must follow a strict structure. We observe that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-only alignment of Speech-LLMs is brittle under dense overlaps, often leading to burst hallucinations and malformed speaker/timestamp tags. We propose a unified two-stage generative framework: (i) CoT-augmented SFT that infers the global speaker count before transcription, and (ii) GRPO-based constrained exploration guided by a Multi-dimensional Constraint-Aware Reward (MCAR) that directly optimizes permutation-invariant accuracy while enforcing counting, temporal, and structural constraints. On Libri3Mix and a Dynamic-Mix (2+3) set (speaker count unknown at test time), our model achieves 14.52%/9.24% cpWER and 1.95%/1.12% WDER, respectively, with GRPO yielding a 35%/54% relative cpWER reduction over SFT+CoT.

items.title: KFC-KWS: Keyframe Fusion with CTC for User-Defined Keyword Spotting
items.authors: Jin Li(Hangzhou Dianzi University); Wenbin Jiang(Hangzhou Dianzi University); Ji Hu(Hangzhou Dianzi University)
items.abstract: User-defined keyword spotting (KWS) enables personalized voice interaction by detecting user-specified keywords. A key challenge in this task is distinguishing target keywords from phonetically confusable alternatives. To address this challenge, we propose KFC-KWS, a multimodal framework that leverages connectionist temporal classification (CTC)-guided keyframe selection. Specifically, we exploit the peaky posterior distributions of CTC to identify high-confidence phoneme frames, enabling precise alignment across audio, phoneme, and text modalities. These keyframes are then fused with full-utterance representations through cross-attention to capture both local discriminative cues and global contextual information. On LibriPhrase, KFC-KWS achieves the best-balanced performance (98.73% AUC) and substantially outperforms advanced baselines on the challenging hard subset (97.65% AUC and 7.75% EER), demonstrating its effectiveness in discriminating between highly confusable keywords.

items.title: Avoiding Catastrophic Forgetting in Text-Only Adaptation of LLM-based ASR via Multi-View Text Denoising
items.authors: Sergio Burdisso(Idiap Research Institute); Esaú Villatoro-Tello(Idiap Research Institute); Thibault Bañeras-Roux(Idiap Research Institute); Shashi Kumar(Idiap Research Institute; EPFL); Srikanth Madikeri(University of Zurich); Pradeep Rangappa(Idiap Research Institute); Manjunath K E(Uniphore); Petr Motlicek(Idiap Research Institute; Brno University of Technology); Andreas Stolcke(Uniphore)
items.abstract: Adapting LLM-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to new domains using text-only data is challenging. Naively fine-tuning the LLM on target text disrupts the speech-text alignment learned by the projector, causing catastrophic forgetting. We propose a lightweight text-only adaptation strategy that formulates adaptation as a denoising task and introduces a multi-view noise-driven batching scheme to preserve alignment. Each mini-batch mixes paired source audio-text examples, projector-induced noisy transcripts, synthetically corrupted source transcripts, and corrupted target transcripts. This mixing enables domain adaptation while maintaining speech-text alignment. Our method requires no architectural changes or additional parameters and achieves up to 25.4% relative WER improvement over the non-adapted base model, outperforming recent text-only adaptation methods.

items.title: AQA-TTRL: Self-Adaptation in Audio Question Answering with Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
items.authors: Haoyu Zhang(The University of Tokyo); Jiaxian Guo(The University of Tokyo); Dong Yang(The University of Tokyo); Yusuke Iwasawa(The University of Tokyo); Yutaka Matsuo(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) exhibit strong capabilities in general audio understanding but remain static after deployment, limiting their adaptability to real-world data. Since supervised fine-tuning is costly, we propose AQA-TTRL, a novel framework for audio understanding that enables on-the-fly evolution via test-time reinforcement learning using only unlabeled test data. It generates pseudo-labels via majority voting and optimizes the model through reinforcement learning. To address the noise in self-generated labels, we introduce confidence weighting to adjust training signals. Furthermore, multiple-attempt sampling mitigates advantage collapse and stabilizes training. Across MMAU, MMAR, and MMSU, AQA-TTRL achieves significant average improvements of 4.42% for Qwen2.5-Omni 7B and 11.04% for the 3B model. Notably, the adapted 3B model outperforms direct inference of the unadapted 7B model, highlighting the effectiveness of test-time adaptation in audio understanding.

items.title: AFG-Bias: Acoustic-Fusion-Gated Biasing for Plug-and-Play Hotword Customization in LLM-Based ASR
items.authors: Long Wu(Qifu Technology); Lingchao Zhao(Qifu Technology); Yuanzhong Zheng(Qifu Technology); Haojun Fei(Qifu Technology); Qing Yang(Qifu Technology)
items.abstract: LLM-based ASR achieves strong transcription but struggles with rare domain-specific entities. Prior biasing methods either require architecture-specific training or rely on prompt injection, which suffers from scale collapse and hallucination. We propose AFG-Bias, a plug-and-play framework grounding hotword biasing in acoustic evidence without modifying LLM parameters. Cross-Modal Acoustic Retrieval (CAR) selects relevant hotwords from a large candidate list via sliding-window alignment, and Acoustic-Fusion Gating injects verified bias into decoding while suppressing hallucinations. On three LLM-ASR backbones, AFG-Bias achieves up to 74.1% relative CER reduction in financial and medical domains, and improves AISHELL-1 hotword F1 by up to 5.4 absolute points.

title: Robust and Real-World ASR Systems
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 10 - Oral 2 - Robust and Real-World ASR Systems

items.title: Decoding the Trade-off: A Large-Scale Analysis of Latency and Stability in LLM-based Speech Translation Cascades
items.authors: Shinyoung Sun(Sogang University); Taehoon Kim(Sogang University)
items.abstract: Real-time subtitling must balance low latency with stable translations. In segment-level cloud cascades, aggressive endpointing increases request rate and can push utilization beyond service capacity, triggering a backlog avalanche in which queueing delay dominates and "fast" settings become slower in steady state. We present RST, a reproducible KO→EN subtitle pipeline that distinguishes time-to-first-text (latency_first) and time-to-stable-text (latency_stable). On the full FLEURS corpus, we show that aggressive endpointing drives cascades into a backlog regime (median RTF > 1), where latency_stable grows over time. Whisper prompt conditioning further degrades short-chunk streaming ASR by +14-17 pp CER and can leak instructions. Sweeps reveal a clear stability boundary. We define an operational threshold as the most aggressive setting with median RTF ≤1, showing that throughput stability is essential for low-latency LLM-based cascades.

items.title: Fed-SpeechLLM: Federated Learning Speech Language Models for Multilingual ASR
items.authors: Mohamed Nabih Ali(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Daniele Falavigna(Fondazione Bruno Kessler); Alessio Brutti(Fondazione Bruno Kessler)
items.abstract: SpeechLLMs show strong promise for multilingual ASR, yet centralized training conflicts with privacy constraints over distributed, linguistically diverse data. This paper presents Fed-SpeechLLM, a federated learning framework for multilingual SpeechLLM-based ASR evaluated on a bilingual English and Italian setting. We study federated optimization under compounded non-IID conditions from acoustic and cross-lingual heterogeneity. Standard FL methods degrade when clients hold language-skewed distributions. Moreover, we propose language-aware gradient aggregation and a sampling clustering-based method to mitigate multilingual imbalance, using selective aggregation of speech encoders and projection layers with a frozen LLM backbone. Results confirm competitive performance against centralized training.

items.title: Multi-Channel Differential ASR for Robust Wearer Speech Recognition on Smart Glasses
items.authors: Yufeng Yang(The Ohio State University); Yiteng Huang(Meta); Yong Xu(Meta); Li Wan(Meta); Suwon Shon(Meta); Yang Liu(Meta); Yifeng Fan(Meta); Zhaojun Yang(Meta); Olivier Siohan(Meta); Yue Liu(Meta); Ming Sun(Meta); Florian Metze(Meta)
items.abstract: With the growing adoption of wearable devices such as smart glasses for AI assistants, wearer speech recognition (WSR) is becoming increasingly critical to next-generation human-computer interfaces. However, in real environments, interference from side-talk speech remains a significant challenge to WSR and may cause accumulated errors for downstream tasks such as natural language processing. In this work, we introduce a novel multi-channel differential automatic speech recognition (ASR) method for robust WSR on smart glasses. The proposed system takes differential inputs from different frontends that complement each other to improve the robustness of WSR, including a beamformer, microphone selection, and a lightweight side-talk detection model. Evaluations on both simulated and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms the traditional approach, achieving up to an 18.0% relative reduction in word error rate.

items.title: ESPnet3: Infrastructure for Scalable Speech and Audio Research in the Foundation Model Era
items.authors: Masao Someki(Carnegie Mellon University); Alexander Polok(Czechia Brno University of Technology); Carlos Carvalho(Portugal Instituto Superior Tecnico); Chyi-Jiunn Lin(Carnegie Mellon University); Da-Hee Yang(Carnegie Mellon University; Hanyang University); Jiatong Shi(Carnegie Mellon University); Jinchuan Tian(Carnegie Mellon University); Nelson Enrique Yalta Soplin(Hitachi Astemo); Samuele Cornell(Carnegie Mellon University); Siddhant Arora(Carnegie Mellon University); Francisco Teixeira(Portugal Instituto Superior Tecnico); Wei Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); William Chen(Carnegie Mellon University); Alberto Abad(Portugal Instituto Superior Tecnico); Chenda Li(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University); Wangyou Zhang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
items.abstract: Recent speech research involves increasingly large datasets, complex models, and diverse experimental workflows. However, existing frameworks require substantial engineering effort to support such experiments. We present ESPnet3, a speech and audio research framework built on a modular system architecture with configuration-driven dataset composition and unified Python-based workflows. ESPnet3 introduces a DataOrganizer abstraction for flexible dataset integration and dataset sharding for memory-efficient large-scale training, while allowing recipe-specific logic through lightweight stage overrides. In OWSM pre-training experiments, ESPnet3 reduces per-epoch training time by 21.1 minutes compared to ESPnet2 and achieves >80% GPU utilization in multi-node training. Fine-tuning experiments show that new models and datasets can be integrated with around 46 lines of additional code. ESPnet3 will be publicly released with model checkpoints and training logs.

items.title: SCRIBE: Diagnostic Evaluation and Rich Transcription Models for Indic ASR
items.authors: Kavya Manohar(Adalat AI); Arghya Bhattacharya(Adalat AI); Kush Juvekar(Adalat AI); Kumarmanas Nethil(Adalat AI)
items.abstract: Automatic speech recognition replaces typing only when correction costs less than manual entry, a threshold determined by error types, not counts: fixing a misrecognized domain term costs far more than inserting a comma. Word error rate (WER) fails on two fronts: it collapses distinct error categories into a single scalar, and it structurally penalizes agglutinative languages where valid sandhi merges inflate scores. We introduce SCRIBE, a diagnostic framework that provides categorical error decomposition into lexical, punctuation, numeral, and domain-entity rates through sandhi-tolerant alignment with domain vocabulary injection. Human validation confirms SCRIBE aligns with expert judgment where WER does not. We release SCRIBE, an LLM curation pipeline, benchmarks, and open-weight rich transcription models for Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada.

items.title: Audio-KWS-Gated Error Memory Retrieval for Incremental ASR Post-Correction
items.authors: Taira Ashikawa(Toshiba Corporation); Daichi Hayakawa(Toshiba Corporation); Takehiko Kagoshima(Toshiba Corporation); Tomoki Watanabe(Toshiba Corporation)
items.abstract: ASR has improved, yet rare and domain-specific terms remain challenging. LLMs enable second-pass post-correction without retraining an ASR model. In long-running use, correction logs can be reused to fix recurring errors, but full-history prompting is limited by the LLM context window, and text-only selection is brittle when trigger terms are misrecognized. We propose an incremental post-correction framework with Audio-KWS-gated retrieval, where Audio-KWS detects keywords from audio to select relevant correction records within the context window. We proceed in three steps: (i) LLM-based error analysis extracts correction pairs to update a keyword inventory, (ii) Audio-KWS runs on audio to detect Top-N keywords and retrieve correction records (using phonetic readings as keywords for Japanese), and (iii) the LLM applies record-guided edits. On Earnings-21 and CSJ, our method achieves about 70% prompt reduction (Top-20 English; Top-10 Japanese) while improving WER/CER and Bias-F1.

title: Speech, Voice and Language Disorders
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 13 - Oral 2 - Speech, Voice and Language Disorders

items.title: Voice Onset Time Categorical Perception in Mandarin-Speaking People Who Stutter: A Zoom-In Nonword Study
items.authors: Yusuke Kiyama(Peking University); Xiyu Wu(Peking University)
items.abstract: As speech production and perception share neural mechanisms, people who stutter (PWS) may also exhibit atypical speech perception. The present study used a nonword continuum and a zoom-in design concentrating stimuli around the category boundary to analyze categorical perception of voice onset time (VOT) in Mandarin-speaking PWS. In identification, PWS showed a trend-level rightward boundary shift, requiring longer VOTs to perceive aspirated consonants. Unlike fluent controls, who displayed typical response delays near the boundary, PWS showed a reduced asymmetry, indicating inefficient access to phonemic categories. In discrimination, accuracy and reaction times did not differ between groups; however, more severe PWS responded faster to within-category stimuli. As accuracy remained stable, this likely reflects right hemisphere compensatory processing. Thus, PWS do not show impaired categorical perception per se but exhibit atypicality in forming and accessing category mappings.

items.title: Learning to Hear Hesitation: Continual Learning for Disfluency-Aware ASR
items.authors: Henri-Leon Kordt(University of Hamburg); Theresa Pekarek Rosin(University of Hamburg); Jae Hee Lee(University of Hamburg); Stefan Wermter(University of Hamburg)
items.abstract: Despite advances in large-scale Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), disfluent speech remains challenging, as state-of-the-art systems are often optimized to omit disfluencies, leading to information loss and hallucinations. Prior work has focused on verbatim transcription and the integration of disfluency markers, but adapting models on limited datasets can lead to catastrophic forgetting of general-domain knowledge. We address this gap by leveraging continual learning (CL) with explicit disfluency tokens. We first introduce these tokens into a pretrained ASR model to establish stable token mechanisms, and then continue training on additional datasets with varying disfluency distributions. Through a detailed analysis of model dynamics during training, we identify a trade-off between marker learning and ASR performance, and a consistent cross-attention head mechanism shared across CL methods.

items.title: Measuring Vocal Efficiency in Daily Life in Patients with Voice Disorders Using Wireless Accelerometer and Microphone Sensors
items.authors: Ahmed Yousef(MGH; Harvard Medical School); Emma Willis(MGH); Vahni Tagirisa(MGH); Robert Hillman(MGH; Harvard Medical School); Daryush Mehta(MGH; Harvard Medical School)
items.abstract: Voice disorders are linked to inefficient phonation, with vocal efficiency (VE) measured in clinic. We studied ecological vocal efficiency (EVE) by estimating daily-life VE as SPL/Ps (dB/dB) using a wireless dual-sensor voice monitor: subglottal pressure (Ps) predicted from a neck-surface accelerometer (ACC) and sound pressure level (SPL) from a microphone. 14 females participated (7 with vocal fold nodules; 7 matched controls). In lab, VE was computed via a /p/-vowel sequence (loud-to-soft; 3 pitch levels). Participants completed 3 days of ambulatory monitoring (12 h/day), and EVE was computed. Patients showed lower EVE and reduced variability than controls in daily life (4.1 vs 4.7, effect size r = 0.67; SD 0.4 vs 1.0, r = 0.91); variability metrics separated groups better in field than in lab. Patients spent significantly more time outside the EVE normative range than controls (92 vs 36%; p = 0.03; r = 0.81). Preliminary results support EVE as an ecological marker of vocal function.

items.title: Mispronunciation Modeling via PPG-Based Phone Editing: A Data Augmentation Framework for Dysarthric Speech Recognition
items.authors: Tsai-Hsiu Ko(National Cheng Kung University); You-Cyuan Jhuo(National Cheng Kung University); Chung-Hsien Wu(National Cheng Kung University)
items.abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems face significant challenges in recognizing dysarthric speech due to severe acoustic variability, frequent mispronunciations, and extreme data scarcity. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel speaker-dependent data augmentation framework utilizing phonetic posteriorgram (PPG)-based phone editing. By quantifying individual pronunciation variations, our method selectively edits the phonetic representations of typical speech to emulate the mispronunciation patterns of target dysarthric speakers. This technique is further integrated with speaking style conversion and phonetic-level speed perturbation to comprehensively capture both the articulatory and prosodic characteristics of dysarthria. We evaluated our approach on the UASpeech corpus by fine-tuning a HuBERT ASR model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively enhances recognition robustness, achieving an overall word error rate of 19.53%.

items.title: Modeling Lombard Effects in Voice Disorders Using Daily-Life Monitoring of Ambient Noise and Voice Acoustics
items.authors: Ahmed M. Yousef(Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard Medical School); Trishul Chowdhury(Massachusetts General Hospital; Northeastern University); Gregory Ciccarelli(MIT Lincoln Laboratory); Thomas F. Quatieri(MIT Lincoln Laboratory); Robert E. Hillman(Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard Medical School); Daryush D. Mehta(Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard Medical School)
items.abstract: Real-world Lombard effects—vocal adjustments in noisy environments—are overlooked in patients with voice disorders. We analyzed ambulatory data from 24 patients with phonotraumatic and non-phonotraumatic vocal hyperfunction (PVH and NPVH) and 18 healthy controls (2–4 days; ≥ 10 h/day), synchronizing equivalent ambient noise levels (Leq) with voice measures: SPL (sound level), F0 (pitch), CPP (cepstral peak prominence), and H1H2 (first minus second harmonic magnitude). We fit models predicting each voice measure from ambient noise (Leq mean, SD). With higher Leq, SPL, F0, and CPP rose and H1H2 fell; CPP showed the strongest correlation (r = 0.36–0.53). Nonlinear models fit best (max test r² = 0.32 for CPP). PVH had steeper SPL slope (0.65 dB/dB Leq mean; 0.86 dB/dB Leq SD) and larger CPP slope (0.18 dB/dB Leq mean) than NPVH. Real-world Lombard effects in patients were subtype-specific, with CPP capturing voice-quality effects beyond SPL and F0.

items.title: A Transcript-anchored Pipeline With Large Language Models For Detecting Inappropriate Pauses In Dysarthric Speech
items.authors: Minsu Han(LG Electronics); Insung Lee(Sogang University); Taeyoung Jeong(Sogang University); Myoung-Wan Koo(Sogang University)
items.abstract: Dysarthria, a motor speech disorder common after stroke, reduces intelligibility and often involves prosodic abnormalities such as inappropriate pauses (IPs). These provide critical cues for clinical assessment and treatment; however, reliable automatic evaluation remains challenging because transcript-level information is essential. We present an automated framework for IP detection using large language models (LLMs). The framework integrates verbatim automatic speech recognition, the Montreal Forced Aligner with refined temporal boundaries, LLM-guided lexical adaptation, and LLM-based classification with rationale generation. This pipeline enables accurate identification of IPs and provides precise time alignment in dysarthric speech. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance against expert evaluation, highlighting the effectiveness of LLM-guided processing. Overall, our study introduces a scalable and explainable approach for clinical and research assessment.
