items.title: Synergizing Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Alzheimer Detection with Language-Invariant Multimodal Bi-Geometric Adversarial Learning
items.authors: Girish (Ulster University); Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar(Ulster University); Farhan Sheth(Manipal University); Muskaan Singh(Ulster University); Juliana Gerard(Ulster University); Paula McClean(Ulster University); Kongfatt Wong-Lin(Ulster University)
items.abstract: In this work, we study zero-shot cross-lingual speech-based Alzheimer's disease detection (SADD). We hypothesize that learning language-invariant multimodal representations by fusing multilingual speech and text pretrained models is essential for reliable transfer to unseen languages, as the two modalities capture complementary acoustic and linguistic markers of cognitive impairment while adversarial learning suppresses language-specific confounds. Empirical results in zero-shot cross-lingual evaluation substantiate the hypothesis, showing that multimodal fusion consistently outperforms unimodal baselines. To this end, we propose ORBIT, a novel framework that combines cross-attentive fusion, multi-tap language adversaries, and complementary spherical-hyperbolic geometric learning with consensus clustering. Across settings, ORBIT achieves the strongest performance compared to unimodal models and simple concatenation-based fusion baselines.

items.title: CoSTA: Cognitive-State-Conditioned TTS Data Augmentation Using ASR Transcripts for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection
items.authors: Yin-Long Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Yuanchao Li(University of Edinburgh); Yiming Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Yue Li(University of Science and Technology of China); Rui Feng(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiaxin Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Shaobo Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Liu He(University of Science and Technology of China); Yuang Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiahong Yuan(University of Science and Technology of China); Zhen-Hua Ling(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: Speech-based Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection is constrained by scarce pathological speech data. To address this, we propose CoSTA, a Text-to-Speech (TTS)-based data augmentation framework. Specifically, we first develop two Cognitive-State-Conditioned (CS-Cond) TTS models by adapting CosyVoice2 and F5-TTS to synthesize speech with distinct AD and Healthy Control characteristics. Furthermore, by constructing a transcript pool comprising Manual Transcripts (MT) and 36 Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) transcripts, we investigate the impact of text sources on TTS-based augmentation. We also perform augmentation-factor analysis and test-time augmentation. Experiments on the ADReSS dataset show that CS-Cond TTS significantly improves synthetic speech utility, and ASR-driven augmentation frequently outperforms MT-driven augmentation. Finally, CoSTA yields a 4.16% gain over the baseline, achieving an audio-only accuracy of 85.83% on the ADReSS test set and outperforming prior methods.

items.title: WSG: Clinically-Informed Weighted Speech Graphs for Dementia Detection
items.authors: Yao Xiao(University of Sheffield); Fritz Peters(University of Sheffield); Madhurananda Pahar(University of Sheffield); Dorota A Braun(University of Sheffield); Caitlin H Illingworth(University of Sheffield); Stefan Goetze(University of Sheffield); Daniel Blackburn(University of Sheffield); Heidi Christensen(University of Sheffield)
items.abstract: Early detection of dementia is critical, yet clinical assessments are often time-consuming and costly. Speech graphs offer a scalable, automated approach by modelling utterances as graphs to capture structural patterns that indicate cognitive decline. While existing methods overlook crucial information such as word meaning and pronunciation, this work proposes Weighted Speech Graphs (WSGs), integrating clinically motivated attributes into speech graphs, and presents a novel graph-derived feature set for dementia detection. Remarkably, just one or two features can achieve performance comparable to a full baseline feature set, while providing interpretable insights aligned with clinical observations. Furthermore, an open-source Python framework for graph construction, feature extraction and visualisation is released, promoting reproducibility and extensibility. Together, these advances bridge practical application and clinical insights in speech graph-based dementia detection.

items.title: Etiology-Aware Speech Language Models for Dysarthric Speech Recognition
items.authors: Moreno La Quatra(Kore University of Enna); Alkis Koudounas(Sony Group Corporation); Valerio Mario Salerno(Kore University of Enna); Sabato Marco Siniscalchi(Università degli Studi di Palermo)
items.abstract: Standard ASR systems ignore clinical context about speakers' neurological conditions, limiting their effectiveness on dysarthric speech. We propose etiology-aware speech language models that incorporate clinical knowledge to improve recognition. We compare four strategies: standard fine-tuning, auxiliary etiology classification, providing the condition as input context (hinting), and predicting the condition before transcribing within the same autoregressive stream. We find that predicting the condition before transcribing is the most effective strategy, achieving 7.77% WER on the Speech Accessibility Project dataset, a 6.4% relative reduction over standard fine-tuning. This approach requires no clinical labels at inference. Auxiliary classification reaches higher etiology accuracy yet fails to reduce WER, showing that clinical reasoning must occur within the generation stream to benefit recognition. Cross-dataset evaluation on TORGO confirms consistent gains across conditions.

items.title: Confidence Score Guided Incremental and Speaker Adaptive Pseudo-Labeling for Semi-Supervised Elderly Speech Recognition
items.authors: Chengxi Deng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xurong Xie(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Shujie Hu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Jiajun Deng(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Mengzhe Geng(National Research Council Canada); Youjun Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Huimeng Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Haoning Xu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Guinan Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xunying Liu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel confidence score guided incremental and speaker adaptive pseudo-labeling approach for semi-supervised elderly speech recognition. It facilitates higher-quality pseudo-label selection and progressive refinement, while also mitigating speaker heterogeneity. A confidence estimation module is designed to rank the reliability of untranscribed data, enabling a curriculum learning trajectory that progressively folds in unlabeled data subsets from high to low confidence. Speaker-specific characteristics are captured through speaker adaptive training with learnable prompts. Experiments on the English DementiaBank Pitt and Cantonese JCCOCC MoCA elderly speech datasets suggest that the proposed method outperforms the semi-supervised baseline using no confidence scores guided incremental or speaker adaptive pseudo-labeling by statistically significant word error rate (WER) or character error rate (CER) reductions of 1.45% and 2.27% absolute (6.21% and 6.98% relative).

items.title: Label Correction Enhanced Dual-Stream Multiple Instance Learning for Weakly-Supervised Depression Detection in Speech
items.authors: Yanfei Sun(Nanjing Univ. Posts & Telecommun.; Wuxi University); Yuanyuan Zhou(Nanjing Univ. Posts & Telecommun.); Xinzhou Xu(Nanjing Univ. Posts & Telecommun.; Graz University of Technology); Jin Qi(Nanjing Univ. Posts & Telecommun.); Feiyi Xu(Nanjing Univ. Posts & Telecommun.); Zhao Ren(University of Bremen); Björn W. Schuller(Technische Universität München; Imperial College London)
items.abstract: Automatic Depression Detection (ADD) in speech aims to estimate speaker's depressive state through speech-based intelligent methods, yet existing speech-based ADD works fail to jointly address inaccurate and inexact labels for ADD in weakly-supervised cases. To this end, we propose an approach of Label Correction enhanced Dual-stream Multiple Instance Learning (LC-DMIL) for weakly-supervised speech-based ADD. The proposed LC-DMIL includes a label correction module focusing on correcting inaccurate labels through fused likelihood-ratio-based and prototype-based correction strategies, and a depression detection module employing a dual-stream multiple instance approach towards the inexact labels. Experiments on weakly-supervised speech-based depression detection data indicate that, the proposed approach performs effectively for the weakly-supervised speech-based ADD.

items.title: QC-GAN: A Parameter-Efficient Quaternion Conformer GAN for High-Fidelity Speech Enhancement
items.authors: Shogo Yamauchi(The Asahi Shimbun Company); Hideaki Tamori(The Asahi Shimbun Company); Makoto Sakai(The Asahi Shimbun Company); Yosuke Yamano(The Asahi Shimbun Company); Tohru Nitta(Tokyo Woman's Christian University)
items.abstract: We propose a parameter-efficient speech enhancement framework, Quaternion Conformer GAN (QC-GAN), which combines a Quaternion Conformer generator with MetricGAN-based training. The Hamilton product encodes the magnitude and phase via structured weight sharing, reducing the number of layer parameters while preserving their interdependencies. A metric-learning discriminator was employed to maximize perceptual quality by optimizing the approximate perceptual evaluation scores. On the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, QC-GAN achieved a Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) score of 3.48 with only 0.89M parameters, delivering a performance comparable to state-of-the-art models at less than half their size. A 35K-parameter variant achieved a PESQ score of 3.23, surpassing conventional methods with significantly fewer parameters. Evaluation on the DNS-Challenge 3 dataset further confirmed generalization to real-world conditions.

items.title: SEMamba++: A General Speech Restoration Framework Leveraging Global, Local, and Periodic Spectral Patterns
items.authors: Yongjoon Lee(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)); Jung-Woo Choi(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST))
items.abstract: General speech restoration demands techniques that can interpret complex speech structures under various distortions. While State-Space Models like SEMamba have advanced the state-of-the-art in speech denoising, they are not inherently optimized for critical speech characteristics, such as spectral periodicity or multi-resolution frequency analysis. In this work, we introduce an architecture tailored to incorporate speech-specific features as inductive biases. In particular, we propose the Global, Local, and Periodic (GLP) module, a frequency feature extraction block that effectively and efficiently leverages the properties of frequency bins. Then, we design a multi-resolution parallel time-frequency dual-processing block to capture diverse spectral patterns, and a learnable mapping to further enhance model performance. With all our ideas combined, the proposed SEMamba++ achieves the best performance among multiple baseline models while remaining computationally efficient.

items.title: ABSE-NET: A Lightweight Neural Model for Active Binaural Speech Enhancement in Open-Fit Hearing Aids
items.authors: De Hu(Inner Mongolia University); Xue Du(Inner Mongolia University); Qingyin Zhao(Inner Mongolia University); Qintuya Si(Inner Mongolia University)
items.abstract: Open-fit hearing aids have attracted growing attention due to their superior wearing comfort. However, the open-fit design inevitably causes acoustic leakage into the ear canal, degrading the performance of existing binaural speech enhancement (BSE). To this end, we propose ABSE-NET, an active BSE framework integrating active noise control (ANC) with BSE to jointly enhance target speech and suppress acoustic leakage. The ABSE-NET pipeline cascades a binaural MVDR (BMVDR) with a lightweight neural network (LNN). The former achieves a coarse BSE, whereas the latter simultaneously cancels acoustic leakage and compensates for BMVDR-induced distortion. The LNN uses an encoder-decoder with a feature fusion module, which includes frequency-time dependency learning and convolutional attention blocks. Unlike traditional BSE+ANC solutions via adaptive filtering, ABSE-NET needs no in-ear microphone in practical deployment. Experiments validate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods. Code repository: https://github.com/Bream101/ABSE-NET.

items.title: A Fast Solver for Interpolating Stochastic Differential Equation Diffusion Models for Speech Restoration
items.authors: Bunlong Lay(University of Hamburg; HITeC Hamburg); Timo Gerkmann(University of Hamburg)
items.abstract: Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs) are a well-established class of diffusion models for unconditional image generation, while SGMSE+ is a well-established conditional diffusion model for speech enhancement. One of the downsides of diffusion models is that solving the reverse process requires many evaluations of a large Neural Network. Although advanced fast sampling solvers have been developed for DPMs, they are not directly applicable to models such as SGMSE+ due to differences in their diffusion processes. Specifically, DPMs transform between the data distribution and a standard Gaussian distribution, whereas SGMSE+ interpolates between the target distribution and a noisy observation. This work first develops a formalism of interpolating Stochastic Differential Equations (iSDEs) that includes SGMSE+, and second proposes a solver for iSDEs. The proposed solver enables fast sampling with as few as 10 Neural Network evaluations across multiple speech restoration tasks.

items.title: Explicit Context-Driven Neural Acoustic Modeling for High-Fidelity RIR Generation
items.authors: Chen Si(University of California San Diego); Qianyi Wu(Monash University); Chaitanya Amballa(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Romit Roy Choudhury(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)
items.abstract: Realistic sound simulation plays a critical role in many applications. A key element in sound simulation is the room impulse response (RIR), which characterizes how sound propagates within a given space. Recent studies have applied neural implicit methods to learn RIR using context information collected from the environment, such as scene images. However, these approaches do not effectively leverage explicit geometric information from the environment. To further exploit neural implicit models with direct geometric features, we present MiNAF, which queries a rough room mesh at given locations and extracts distance distributions as an explicit representation of local context. Our approach demonstrates that incorporating explicit local geometric features can better guide the model in generating more accurate RIR predictions. Through comparisons with conventional and state-of-the-art methods, we show that MiNAF performs competitively across various evaluation metrics.

items.title: SCNet: Enhancing GAN-based Speech Generation with Subband Condition Network and Magnitude-aware Phase Loss
items.authors: Nan Xu(Tencent); Mingxue Yang(UESTC‌)
items.abstract: Recent speech generation has been predominantly driven by GAN-based networks aimed at high-quality waveform synthesis from mel-spectrograms. However, these methods often operate as black-box models, leading to the loss of inherent spectral information. In this work, we propose SCNet, a GAN-based vocoder augmented with a Subband Condition Network to address this issue. Specifically, SCNet leverages a subband signal predicted by a lightweight condition network as prior knowledge. This subband signal is then transformed via STFT to obtain Fourier coefficients, which are integrated into the backbone for the enhanced reconstruction. Additionally, to mitigate the phase wrapping, we introduce a magnitude-aware phase loss that computes instantaneous phase errors weighted by the corresponding magnitude, emphasizing regions with higher energy. Experimental results demonstrate that SCNet achieves superior performance in both objective and subjective evaluations for high-quality speech generation.

items.title: The Role of Laryngeal Position in the Articulation of American English Velar Stop Consonants
items.authors: Daejin Kim(University of New Mexico)
items.abstract: This study re-examines the articulation of voiceless /k/ and voiced /ɡ/ velar stop consonants in American English (AE) by modeling movements of the hyoid bone (HY) and the tongue dorsum (TD) as articulatory gestures using dynamic analysis of ultrasound tongue recordings and multivariate statistical inference methods. HY was found to raise and advance for /k/ and lower and retract for /ɡ/ when TD reaches its target, both of which correlate with the high f0 peak for /k/ and the low f0 peak for /ɡ/ during their following and preceding vowels. /ɡ/ was produced with longer, larger, and faster TD raising toward the velar surface, indicating that /ɡ/ is conditioned by the full spatiotemporal expansion of the tongue with the maximal linguovelar contact. This study suggests that varying degrees of expansion of the tongue, linguovelar contact, and laryngeal positioning simultaneously condition the articulation of AE velar stops, all of which relate to their acoustic correlates.

items.title: Band-Limited Cepstral Analysis of Speaker Sensitivity in Forensic Voice Comparison
items.authors: Shunichi Ishihara(Australian National University); Satoru Tsuge(Daido University); Frantz Clermont(Australian National University)
items.abstract: This study investigates where speaker-sensitive frequency regions (sub-bands) are located and how much speaker-discriminative information each region encodes. Likelihood-ratio-based forensic voice comparison experiments were conducted using Band-Limited Cepstral Coefficient (BLCC) matrices derived from a systematic scan of the 0–8 kHz full-band range with 0.6 kHz and 1.2 kHz sub bands. Approximately 30 seconds of running speech from 162 native male Australian English speakers were analysed. The results show that although all sub-bands contain useful speaker-specific information, frequencies above approximately 7kHz are the least informative, while the 0–0.6 kHz and 4–6 kHz regions provide strong speaker discriminative cues. The findings also illustrate the effectiveness of the BLCC method in accessing and analysing any local spectral region of interest.

items.title: Speaker-Specific and Language-Dependent Temporal Organization in Bilingual Political Speech
items.authors: Nina Hosseini-Kivanani(University of Luxembourg; Radio Télévision Luxembourg); Nafiseh Taghva(Shiraz University); Peter Gilles(University of Luxembourg); Oliver Niebuhr(University of Southern Denmark)
items.abstract: Speech rhythm helps structure persuasive speech, but most empirical work examines monolingual English. This study asks how politicians organize timing when speaking Luxembourgish and French. We analyze 400 sentences from ten politicians, annotated for segments and pauses. We compute rhythm metrics, including means, variability, and pairwise variability indices for consonants and vowels. We quantify speaker and language contributions and test within-speaker language effects with paired t-tests. Results show that consonant-based metrics retain speaker-specific signatures, whereas vowel-based metrics are largely driven by language choice. French tokens display longer and more variable vowels and vocalic intervals, while consonant timing differences are smaller. No robust language by gender interactions emerge. These findings show that language choice systematically reorganizes rhythmic timing in bilingual public speech.

items.title: Revisiting the NZE front vowel shift: evidence from New Zealand's largest and most linguistically diverse city
items.authors: Brooke Ross(University of Auckland); Catherine Watson(University of Auckland); Elaine Ballard(University of Auckland); Miriam Meyerhoff(University of Oxford)
items.abstract: Auckland is New Zealand's largest and most demographically diverse city, yet it has been largely ignored in research on New Zealand English (NZE). Recent work on Modern NZE in Auckland and the rediscovery of key historical commentary suggests the city has played a role in leading sound changes that make NZE distinct. This data also raises questions about the trajectory of NZE's much-discussed Short Front Vowel Shift. This paper explores 100 years of sound change in Auckland through a preliminary acoustic and statistical analysis of NZE's iconic /e, æ, ɪ/ vowels. We compare contemporary Aucklanders' (n=67) speech across two age groups with that of historical Aucklanders (n=8), integrating real and apparent-time analyses. Results show a rise and subsequent fall of /e/ and /æ/ over time, and early centralisation of /ɪ/ among historical speakers, contrasting previous research. Further investigation suggests /ɪ/ centralisation was initially phonologically conditioned by adjacent laterals.

items.title: Effects of body position on vowel formants in New Zealand English
items.authors: Qing Guan(The University of Auckland); Catherine I. Watson(The University of Auckland); C. T. Justine Hui(The University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Speech is produced in everyday contexts that involve different body positions, yet body position is rarely modelled in acoustic analyses. This study tests whether static body position (supine, sitting, standing) affects vowel formants F1 and F2 in New Zealand English using a within-speaker /hVd/ list (11 vowels) from 9 speakers. Linear mixed-effects models with vowel, age, and sex show small position-related differences, with the clearest contrasts involving supine relative to sitting and standing. Position effects vary by vowel, age, and sex. Vowel-specific contrasts are significant for a small subset of vowels, most clearly in high-front categories for F2. In this dataset, F1 position differences are clearer for female speakers, and F2 position differences are significant in the younger female condition. These findings suggest that body position should be documented when interpreting or combining vowel-formant measurements across recording configurations.

items.title: From onset to coda: spectral variation in normative Polish /s/ produced by children
items.authors: Joanna Walczak(Silesian University of Technology); Oliwia Skórzewska(Silesian University of Technology); Zuzanna Miodońska(Silesian University of Technology)
items.abstract: Sibilant fricatives are shaped by multiple linguistic and developmental factors, yet word-position effects in perceptually normative Polish /s/ remain underdescribed. This pilot study examines whether word-initial, word-medial, and word-final positions are associated with acoustic differences in /s/ produced by Polish-speaking preschool children aged 5-8 years. The dataset comprised 816 /s/ tokens from 102 children. Acoustic measures included spectral centroid (CoG), skewness, kurtosis, and spectral flux. Word position significantly affected the spectral properties of /s/: the strongest pairwise differences was present within word-initial and word-medial tokens (CoG, spectral flux, kurtosis, skewness), whereas medial-final contrasts were generally smaller and often non-significant, except for skewness.

items.title: Multi-Level Privacy-Preserving Dementia Detection from Speech via Targeted Adversarial Obfuscation and Representation Learning
items.authors: Henriette Flore Kenne(University of Massachusetts Lowell); Raphael Anaadumba(University of Massachusetts Lowell); Mohammad Arif Ul Alam(University of Massachusetts Lowell)
items.abstract: Speech recordings used for dementia detection inherently expose speaker identity, raising critical privacy concerns. Existing methods typically address only singular threats and fail to resolve the privacy–utility trade-off. We propose a multi-level framework designed to neutralize two distinct eavesdropping vectors. At the signal level, a Cumulative Signal Attack (CSA) concentrates perturbations in keyword-aligned regions to maximize transcription error (Word Error Rate WER = 1.00) while preserving vital prosodic biomarkers. At the feature level, a Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) with Mutual Information (MI)-guided noise injection suppresses speaker-discriminative dimensions while retaining dementia-relevant diagnostic structure. Evaluated on the DementiaBank Pitt Corpus, our framework achieves near-chance speaker identification (Equal Error Rate EER = 0.59, F1 = 0.003) while maintaining strong dementia classification performance (F1 = 0.78, AUC = 0.86).

items.title: An Acoustic Investigation of Mid Front Vowel Harmony in Assamese
items.authors: Saurabh Nath(The Australian National University); Rosey Billington(The Australian National University); Danielle Barth(The Australian National University)
items.abstract: Previous descriptions of Assamese have reported a pattern of vowel harmony in which a mid vowel is raised when followed by a close vowel in the subsequent syllable. Articulatory studies based on a single dialect have offered mixed findings, and systematic acoustic studies remain limited. This study provides an acoustic analysis of /ɛ/-raising in harmonic contexts across the three major dialect regions of Assamese. The data were drawn from 18 adult speakers (3 male and 3 female speakers per region), including both wordlist and connected speech recordings. F1 and F2 measurements were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with harmonic context, vowel duration, dialect, speech style, and gender as predictors. The results show consistent /ɛ/-raising in harmonic contexts across dialects. Although the harmony effect was evident across all dialects and speech styles, its magnitude varied across dialect–style combinations, particularly in vowel height (F1).

title: Behavioral, Cross-lingual, and Multimodal Speech Analysis

items.title: Automatic Detection of Stress from Speech in the Trier Social Stress Test
items.authors: Hanna Drimalla(Bielefeld University); Wieland R. Cremer(Bielefeld University); Christine Kraus(Bielefeld University); Oliver T. Wolf(Ruhr University Bochum)
items.abstract: Automatically detecting stress in speech provides an unobtrusive way to gain insights relevant to behavioral research or clinical assessment. This study investigates the automatic differentiation between a stressful and non-stressful situation, and the prediction of physiological and affective stress responses. Speech data was collected from 50 participants who either completed the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) or a non-stressful control condition. With a processing pipeline that included speaker diarization and machine learning models, we achieved stress detection performance significantly above a mean baseline. Moreover, relevant physiological and affective stress responses were partially predictable from acoustic-prosodic features. Feature-importance analyses identified the most informative predictors contributing to model performance. The findings demonstrate that speech can serve as a meaningful and unobtrusive indicator of multiple dimensions of the human stress response.

items.title: Looking for Affect in Spontaneous Finnish Speech through Linguistic Interpretability
items.authors: Kalle Lahtinen(Tampere University); Liisa Mustanoja(Tampere University); Okko Räsänen(Tampere University)
items.abstract: Existing research on affect in speech has shown how acoustic surface characteristics and content-related linguistic aspects of speech both relate to perceived emotional arousal and valence. However, it is not clear what the relative contributions of these two factors are in the perceptual process. This is especially true for Finnish, for which most existing studies focus on either acoustic-phonetic or text analysis. This paper presents a study where we systematically explore the combinatory role of text- and audio-based features in modeling the human perception of valence and arousal using a newly released affective speech corpus for spontaneous Finnish. We show that the combination of text- and audio-based features improves valence regression results over the individual modalities, whereas for arousal regression the complementary effect is not substantial. The results support prior findings from other languages, providing new data and knowledge on spontaneous Finnish speech.

items.title: Umm... With Transformers? Insights from Filled Pause Use across Four Slavic Parliaments
items.authors: Ivan Porupski(Jožef Stefan Institute); Branimir Dropuljić(TransUnion; University of Zagreb); Nikola Ljubešić(Jožef Stefan Institute; University of Ljubljana; Institute of Contemporary History)
items.abstract: Filled pauses (FPs) are a universal feature of spontaneous speech, yet most studies rely on small, single-language corpora, limiting the generalisability of their findings. We analyse ~4,000 hours of parliamentary speech across four related Slavic languages (Croatian, Czech, Polish, Serbian). FP occurrence is obtained via transformer-based automatic detection, while FP rate is modelled using Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) with Mundlak correction to distinguish within-from between-speaker effects. We replicate a negative association of age and speech rate with FP rate, but find that gender effects are language-specific and directionally opposite to most prior literature. Novel analyses of sentiment, political orientation, and power status reveal a consistent positive association between sentiment and FP rate, alongside parliament-specific modulation by orientation and power status, with opposition speakers tending toward lower FP rates than governing coalition speakers.

items.title: Eye and Mouth Cues in Audiovisual Perception of Mandarin Irony: Evidence from Eye-tracking and Facial Masking
items.authors: Shifeng Xia(Nanjing University of Science and Technology); Shanpeng Li(Nanjing University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Irony is a form of nonliteral language whose comprehension involves integrating auditory and visual cues. Although prosodic cues have been widely studied across languages, the role of facial cues remains underexplored. This study investigated perceptual strategies for different facial regions in decoding Mandarin ironic speech. 44 native speakers completed a perception experiment including ironic blame and praise and their literal counterparts under Visual-only, Audiovisual (quiet), and Audiovisual (noise) conditions. Eye-tracking measured fixation duration and pupil dilation. Results showed distinct visual patterns: ironic blame elicited longer fixations on the eyes, with no pupil-size differences across regions, whereas ironic praise prompted greater attention to the mouth across modalities, with larger pupil size during eye fixations in the quiet audiovisual condition. These findings reveal asymmetric visual processing across irony types and inform multimodal intention recognition.

items.title: Do Speech Emphasis Models Generalize across Languages and Emotions?
items.authors: Megan Wei(Adobe Research; Brown University); Deepali Aneja(Adobe Research); Jiaqi Su(Adobe Research); Yunyun Wang(Adobe Research); Haonan Chen(Adobe Research); Zeyu Jin(Adobe Research)
items.abstract: Prosodic emphasis varies across languages, emotions, and speaking styles, yet existing emphasis detection models are largely trained and evaluated on monolingual neutral read speech. We introduce MMEE (Multilingual Multi-Emotion Emphasis), a corpus of 10,000 professionally recorded expressive utterances (14.13 hours) across 7 languages and 34 emotion/style categories, with three-level perceptual labels (10 annotations per sample). We benchmark two state-of-the-art architectures under monolingual, cross-lingual, multilingual, cross-emotion, cross-dataset, and data-scale settings. Monolingual models show limited zero-shot transfer, degrading across typologically distant languages, while multilingual training substantially improves robustness. Models transfer robustly between high- and low-arousal emotions; bidirectional transfer between synthetic and perceptual benchmarks suggests shared prosodic structure; and performance stays robust even at smaller training scales.

items.title: KuralHub: Exposing Typological Capability Frontiers in Multilingual Speech Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Luxshan Thavarasa(University of Moratuwa); Jubeerathan Thevakumar(University of Moratuwa); Thanikan Sivatheepan(University of Moratuwa); Uthayasanker Thayasivam(University of Moratuwa)
items.abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) advancements are constrained by high-resource bias, limiting global access. To address this, we introduce KuralHub, an open-science initiative democratizing SER for under-resourced languages. We evaluate 11 self-supervised models (WavLM, HuBERT, Wav2vec 2.0, Whisper) across 33 datasets in 29 diverse languages. Beyond standard benchmarking, our study reveals a critical typological bias: cross-lingual transferability is dictated more by structural linguistic properties than pre-training data volume. While models easily adapt to Mandarin or Amharic, they systematically fail on the Dravidian family. Crucially, we demonstrate that simply scaling model parameters fails to resolve this bottleneck. By exposing these linguistic capability frontiers, KuralHub provides a vital roadmap for developing equitable, typologically-aware speech technologies for all speakers.

items.title: YUE-PUB-Speech: A Speech-based Pragmatic Understanding Benchmark for Cantonese
items.authors: Yajie Wen(South China Normal University); Ziwei Gong(Columbia University); Chengyan Wu(South China Normal University; Sun Yat-sen University); Xiyun Gong(Guangzhou College of Commerce); Yun Xue(South China Normal University); Julia Hirschberg(Columbia University); Bolei Ma(LMU Munich & Munich Center for Machine Learning)
items.abstract: Pragmatic understanding is essential for natural human communication, yet most existing studies focus on text-only settings. In this paper we introduce YUE-PUB-Speech, the first multimodal pragmatic dataset for Cantonese, a low-resource language, constructed by sampling pragmatically rich texts and recording corresponding speech by trained annotators. The corpus provides paired text-speech instances that capture pragmatic meaning in spoken language without requiring fine-grained phonological or word-level alignment. Baseline experiments show that incorporating speech signals improves pragmatic understanding compared to text-only models, highlighting the importance of multimodal resources for pragmatic research in speech and language processing.

items.title: TIMBRE: Layer-Wise Cross-Lingual Speech Emotion Recognition Across 49 Layers and 26 Corpora
items.authors: Anatoly Marchenko(Independent Researcher)
items.abstract: We present the first large-scale layer-wise cross-lingual speech emotion recognition analysis: 49 layers of wav2vec2-xls-r-1b across 26 corpora, 23 languages and 14 families, a 49×26×26 tensor of 31,850 experiments. Under linear probing of mean-pooled representations, cross-corpus transfer peaks at layer 15 (31% depth, F1=0.392), the CRIS layer, and collapses by 24.6% at layer 45. Typology is associated with the shape of the layer profile: Romance languages show a U-shaped relative advantage, and the tonal advantage grows with depth. On the same 26×26 matrix with identical classifiers, mean-pooled wav2vec2 outperforms 27-dim acoustic features by 41% (F1: 0.355 vs. 0.252); acoustic features retain 71% of this baseline at a 3.7×10^7-fold lower complexity and prevail on only 3 of 26 corpora. Per-corpus expressiveness and elicitation style, rather than group or family membership, drive overall transferability.

items.title: Hearing Smiles in the Crowd: How Babble Noise Shapes Smiled Speech Perception
items.authors: Rong Li(University of Twente); Esther Janse(Radboud University); Dirk Heylen(University of Twente); Khiet Truong(Radboud University; University of Twente)
items.abstract: In everyday communication, the auditory perception of smiled speech can be hindered by noise. We examined how multi-talker babble noise affected human auditory perception of smile-like speech, consisting of affective amused and mechanical spread-lip speech. Listeners completed two categorization tasks: 1) smile-like detection (smile-like vs. neutral speech) and, within smile-like speech, 2) smile-type categorization (amused vs. spread-lip speech). Results showed that increasing noise reduced perceptual sensitivity in both tasks while systematically altering response bias. In Task 1, as noise increased, participants' accuracy not only decreased but they were also less inclined to report hearing a smile. Similarly, in Task 2, an initial bias toward "amused" responses in quiet reversed under strong noise. These findings demonstrate that smile perception in noise reflects not only degraded sensory evidence but also adaptive shifts in decision strategy under uncertainty.

items.title: Stress Detection Across Daily Activities: A Context-Aware Multimodal Framework with Trajectory and Ambient Speech
items.authors: Wei-Heng Huang(National Tsing Hua University); Woan-Shiuan Chien(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Chi-Chun Lee(National Tsing Hua University)
items.abstract: Stress detection is widely studied for mental health monitoring, with most approaches relying on physiological signals such as HRV. These methods require wearable devices, limiting scalability in practical deployment. Audio signals, particularly speech, provide a non-intrusive alternative, yet models relying solely on sound lack robustness across contexts. Stress perception is inherently context-dependent and influenced by spatial factors beyond speech alone, especially for hospital workers in high-pressure clinical environments. This study proposes a context-aware framework extracting distinct features from speech and mobility trajectories. By employing a late fusion mechanism to combine vocal and movement embeddings, the proposed approach improves robustness, outperforming unimodal audio baselines on a hospital worker dataset. Experimental results show the framework improves the F1 score by 9.32% and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) by 0.038 over the audio-only baseline.

items.title: T-ORR: Text-Anchored Orthogonal Residual Rectification for Robust Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
items.authors: Qi Chen(Tianjin Foreign Studies University); Junyi Chen(Beijing Language and Culture University); Jiabin Han(Tianjin Foreign Studies University); Hongjiao Yang(Tianjin Foreign Studies University)
items.abstract: Sarcasm relies on a covert contradiction between intended connotation and literal text. In Multimodal Sarcasm Detection (MSD), conventional fusion models often obscure sparse incongruity cues by entangling features within a joint space. We propose Text-Anchored Orthogonal Residual Rectification (T-ORR), reframing MSD as a signal separation problem. T-ORR utilizes Dynamic Locality-Constrained Alignment to adaptively focus non-verbal streams on the specific words they modify. A Structure-Preserving Geometric Decomposition then employs QR projection to disentangle these signals into semantic Resonance and modality-specific Dissonance. Rather than standard fusion, a Contrastive Incongruity Routing (CIR) mechanism models the semantic distance between literal and incongruous states. Evaluations on MUStARD and MUStARD++ yield state-of-the-art results, suggesting geometric decoupling effectively isolates multimodal incongruities.

items.title: VerAno: Speaker Anonymization via Self-Supervised Tokenization and Conditional Flow Matching
items.authors: Ngoc Hung Le(Soongsil University); Thien-Phuc Doan(Soongsil University); Thien An Nguyen(Soongsil University); Kyujin Kim(Soongsil University); Souhwan Jung(Soongsil University)
items.abstract: Effective speaker anonymization faces a critical bottleneck: balancing robust privacy protection with the preservation of downstream utility. To resolve this trade-off, we introduce VerAno, a novel framework that leverages a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) to tokenize Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) speech features. By strategically constraining codebook size, VerAno achieves the self-supervised disentanglement of speaker-specific features from speaker-independent features. These discrete tokens are fused with pretrained speaker embeddings and processed by a flow-matching transformer to synthesize high-fidelity acoustic representations. Experimental evaluations on the VoicePrivacy Challenge datasets demonstrate that VerAno substantially outperforms baseline models. Furthermore, the system generalizes favorably across languages, demonstrating promising cross-lingual capabilities when applied to unseen data.

items.title: Controlled Generation of Synthetic Speaker Vectors for Voice Anonymization
items.authors: Ekaterina Kolos(University of Stuttgart); Sarina Meyer(Institute for Natural Language Processing, University of Stuttgart); Ngoc Thang Vu(Institute for Natural Language Processing, University of Stuttgart)
items.abstract: Voice anonymization benefits from transparent control over the pseudo-speaker's voice. Anonymization approaches based on resynthesis substitute the original speaker vector with a different, often artificial, vector, but this does not allow for controlling which original speaker attributes are preserved. To address this, we extend one existing WGAN-based artificial vector generation method with attribute-label conditioning. We also introduce diffusion models as a robust alternative for generating speaker vectors, utilizing classifier guidance for label-informed synthesis. Evaluated using the Voice Privacy Challenge 2024 suite, both approaches demonstrate strong attribute control while maintaining competitive privacy and utility. Furthermore, we propose measures for diversity, originality, and naturalness of synthesized embeddings. Combined with TTS performance on challenging speech, these measures enable the selection of optimal generator configurations for the anonymization pipeline.

items.title: Child-Centric Voice Anonymization in Single and Multi-Speaker Speech via Domain-Adapted SSL Models
items.authors: Pranav Tushar(Singapore Institute of Technology); Xiao Xiao Miao(Duke Kunshan University); Rong Tong(Singapore Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Voice anonymization aims to protect speaker identity while preserving linguistic content and speech usability. However, most anonymization systems are developed on adult speech, leading to degraded performance when applied to child speech. This paper investigates child-centric anonymization by adapting a self-supervised learning (SSL) based anonymization pipeline to the child speech domain. The system is adapted using child speech from the MyST corpus and evaluated under both single-speaker and two-speaker mixture conditions. Experimental results show that child-domain adaptation improves intelligibility and perceptual quality while maintaining strong privacy protection. Extending the approach to multi-speaker further demonstrates that combining target speaker extraction with child-adapted anonymization provides privacy protection while preserving conversational structure. These findings highlight the importance of child-specific adaptation for practical speech anonymization systems.

items.title: Reducing Speaker Residual by Considering Pinhole Effect in Voice Anonymization
items.authors: Zeyan Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Weili Jiang(Ministry of Public Security); Liping Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Boyu Zhao(Ministry of Public Security); Kai Gao(Ministry of Public Security); Zhenhua Ling(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: Voice anonymization aims to protect privacy by suppressing speaker identity while preserving linguistic content and prosody. However, residual speaker attributes in non-identity representations may still increase linkability and weaken privacy protection. To this end, this paper proposes a fine-tuning strategy with a pinhole loss for well-trained voice anonymization frameworks to further reduce residual speaker attributes. Inspired by the pinhole effect, the pinhole loss measures the linkability of anonymized utterances from the same source speaker. By minimizing this loss, linkability is reduced, thereby improving privacy protection. Experiments on multiple anonymization frameworks, pseudo-speaker generation methods, and datasets show improved privacy protection while maintaining utility. Audio samples can be found in https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Pinhole-loss-fine-tunning-4628.

items.title: StreamVoiceAnon+: Emotion-Preserving Streaming Speaker Anonymization via Frame-Level Acoustic Distillation
items.authors: Nikita Kuzmin(Nanyang Technological University; A*STAR); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University)
items.abstract: We address the challenge of preserving emotional content in streaming speaker anonymization (SA). Neural audio codec language models trained for audio continuation tend to degrade source emotion: content tokens discard emotional information, and the model defaults to dominant acoustic patterns rather than preserving paralinguistic attributes. We propose supervised finetuning with neutral-emotion utterance pairs from the same speaker, combined with frame-level emotion distillation on acoustic token hidden states. All modifications are confined to finetuning, which takes less than 2 hours on 4 GPUs and adds zero inference latency overhead, while maintaining a competitive 180ms streaming latency. On the VoicePrivacy 2024 protocol, our approach achieves a 49.2% UAR (emotion preservation) with 5.77% WER (intelligibility), a +24% relative UAR improvement over the baseline (39.7%→49.2%) and +10% over the emotion-prompt variant (44.6% UAR), while maintaining strong privacy (EER 49.0%).1

items.title: Personal Attribute Leakage in Federated Speech Models
items.authors: Hamdan Al-Ali(MBZUAI); Ali Reza Ghavamipour(Maastricht University); Tommaso Caselli(University of Groningen); Fatih Turkmen(University of Groningen); Zeerak Talat(University of Edinburgh); Hanan Aldarmaki(MBZUAI)
items.abstract: Federated learning is a method proposed for privacy-preserving training of machine learning models. In this paper, we analyze the vulnerability of ASR models to attribute inference attacks in the federated setting. We test a non-parametric white-box attack method under a passive threat model on three ASR models: Wav2Vec2, HuBERT, and Whisper. The attack operates solely on weight differentials without access to raw speech from target speakers. We demonstrate attack feasibility on sensitive demographic and clinical attributes: gender, age, accent, emotion, and impaired speech. Our findings indicate that attributes that are underrepresented or absent in the pre-training data are more vulnerable to such inference attacks. In particular, information about accents can be reliably inferred from all models. Our findings expose previously undocumented vulnerabilities in federated ASR models and offer insights towards improved security.

items.title: A Large-Scale Per-Speaker Analysis of Re-identification Risk in Speech Anonymization
items.authors: Orane Dufour(Université de Lorraine); Paul Magron(Université de Lorraine); Mickael Rouvier(Avignon University); Emmanuel Vincent(Université de Lorraine)
items.abstract: Speech anonymization is commonly evaluated using average-case metrics such as the equal error rate, which can hide large disparities in re-identification risks across individuals. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale per-speaker privacy analysis using a linkability-based metric under a worst-case scenario. Nearly 5,000 speakers are evaluated across multiple anonymization systems, attacker architectures, and conversation lengths. While linkability scores are highly polarized at the speaker level, the sets of easy to re-identify and hard to re-identify speakers vary substantially across configurations. We show that no single factor explains speaker vulnerability. Instead, the re-identification risk emerges from the interaction between the attacker, the anonymizer, and the amount of available speech. These results challenge the notion of intrinsic speaker-level privacy risks and emphasize the need for evaluation protocols that are explicitly conditioned on the attacker and anonymizer.

items.title: Privacy-Preserving Speaker Verification with Multi-Granularity Feature Obfuscation
items.authors: Hanseul Kim(Chosun University); Nam In Park(National Forensic Service); Chanjun Chun(Chosun University; Glosori Inc.)
items.abstract: To counter eavesdropping threats from recent advances in speech technology, this paper proposes a privacy-preserving speaker verification (SV) framework that protects both linguistic content and biometric identity. We leverage FAcodec to explicitly remove content-bearing information and selectively apply multi-granularity feature obfuscation to the remaining noncontent representations, preserving speaker-discriminative cues while discouraging faithful waveform reconstruction. Our results further indicate that ASR-based metrics such as Word Error Rate (WER) alone may not fully reflect perceptual privacy: even without content tokens, reconstructed speech can remain partially intelligible to listeners despite high WER. By substantially reducing perceptual intelligibility, our approach achieves an EER of 2.35% on VoxCeleb1-O, a 54.7% relative improvement over prior state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating a favorable balance between biometric utility and linguistic privacy.

items.title: Imperceptible Voiceprint Protection via Human-Machine Perception Discrepancy Feature Disentanglement
items.authors: Chenlong Xue(Army Engineering University of PLA); Meng Sun(Army Engineering University of PLA); Qiang Zhang(Army Engineering University of PLA); Xiongwei Zhang(Army Engineering University of PLA); Kunyuan Li(Army Engineering University of PLA); Yuan Liao(Chinese University of Hong Kong); Xiaoyi Ge(Information Support Force Engineering University); Kui Yao(Army Engineering University of PLA)
items.abstract: The proliferation of zero-shot voice cloning models increases the risk of unauthorized speaker impersonation. Although adversarial perturbation provides an effective defense, existing methods face a fundamental trade-off: strong perturbations introduce audible artifacts, while imperceptible ones may lack robustness when transferred to unseen systems. We introduce a two-stage framework exploiting human-machine perception discrepancy. We first train a disentanglement network to separate content and speaker information, then inject perturbations into the speaker embedding space where machines are sensitive but humans are not. Experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves 87.2% defense success rate, surpassing state-of-the-art embedding-level defenses by 7%, while maintaining a high MOS of 4.18 and demonstrating strong transferability to black-box voice cloning systems.

items.title: Towards Privacy-Preserving ASR: Speaker-Level Machine Unlearning
items.authors: Seaone Ok(Seoul National University); Seungu Han(Seoul National University); Eungbeom Kim(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)
items.abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are commonly designed to transcribe linguistic content independently of speaker identity. However, speaker-specific information can persist within the latent representations of ASR models, raising privacy concerns when training data includes sensitive individuals. While machine unlearning has been studied in several speech tasks, applying speaker unlearning to ASR remains challenging due to the strong entanglement of linguistic and speaker-related information in speech representations. In this work, we conduct a layer-wise analysis of Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) based ASR representations, revealing that speaker identity is primarily encoded in intermediate encoder layers. Based on this observation, we explore a feature-level unlearning strategy that targets these identity structures. Experiments on the VCTK corpus show that the proposed approach removes the influence of specific speakers while maintaining robust transcription performance.

items.title: NaVo: Natural Voice Protection against Voice Cloning Attacks via Generative Universal Adversarial Audio
items.authors: Seoyoung Park(Soongsil University); Seungmin Kim(Soongsil University); Sohee Park(Soongsil University); Dain Kim(Soongsil University); Thien An Nguyen(Soongsil University); Thien-Phuc Doan(Soongsil University); Souhwan Jung(Soongsil University); Daeseon Choi(Soongsil University)
items.abstract: Proactive defense against voice cloning disrupts synthesis by injecting adversarial perturbations. However, prior methods rely on iterative optimization, often causing perceptual distortion and high latency that limit real-time deployment. We propose NaVo, a generative framework that produces natural-sounding universal adversarial audio. NaVo guides a latent diffusion–based text-to-audio model with fine-tuned low-rank adaptation modules tailored to gender and acoustic categories such as rain, music, and babble, enabling high-fidelity, speaker-independent adversarial audio generation. Unlike optimization-based approaches, NaVo supports real-time protection through simple audio mixing without gradient-based inference. It achieves a 76% defense success rate against a widely used commercial voice cloning system in a black-box setting. By jointly addressing universality, audio quality, and computational efficiency, NaVo offers a practical solution for proactive voice protection.

items.title: DAST: A Dual-Stream Voice Anonymization Attacker with Staged Training
items.authors: Ridwan Arefeen(Singapore Institute of Technology); Xiaoxiao Miao(Duke Kunshan University); Rong Tong(Singapore Institute of Technology); Timothy Liu(NVIDIA AI Technology Centre); Aik Beng Ng(NVIDIA AI Technology Centre); Simon See(NVIDIA AI Technology Centre)
items.abstract: Voice anonymization masks vocal traits while preserving linguistic content, which may still leak speaker-specific patterns. To assess and strengthen privacy evaluation, we propose a dual-stream attacker that fuses spectral and self-supervised learning features via parallel encoders with a three-stage training strategy. Stage I establishes foundational speaker-discriminative representations. Stage II leverages the shared identity-transformation characteristics of voice conversion and anonymization, exposing the model to diverse converted speech to build cross-system robustness. Stage III provides lightweight adaptation to target anonymized data. Results on the VoicePrivacy Attacker Challenge (VPAC) dataset demonstrate that Stage II is the primary driver of generalization, enabling strong attacking performance on unseen anonymization datasets. With Stage III, fine-tuning on only 10% of the target anonymization dataset surpasses current state-of-the-art attackers in terms of EER.1 .
